Q7296.t: Africa's rooftop, a snowy island above the plains
Q7296.s: Kilimanjaro belongs to no range: it rises alone, a broad dark volcano swelling out of the savanna. Its summit, Uhuru Peak on the Kibo cone, is 5,895 m high — the top of Africa, yet still about five kilometres below you. Look for the white rim of ice on Kibo, shrinking year by year but still there, just three degrees south of the equator.
Q7296.w: A vast lone dome with a flat, white-streaked top and the jagged Mawenzi peak on its east flank, near the Kenya border.
f: Kilimanjaro is built from three volcanic cones: Kibo, Mawenzi and Shira.
It is the highest free-standing mountain in the world, rising about 4,900 m above the plains at its base.
Its ice fields have shrunk by more than 80% since the early 20th century.

q.q: Which of Kilimanjaro's three volcanic cones holds its summit?

Q39231.t: Japan's lone volcano, white-capped and nearly symmetrical
Q39231.s: On a clear day Fuji is unmistakable: one broad, even cone standing by itself west of Tokyo, its upper slopes white from autumn to spring. It last erupted in 1707. The summit, 3,776 m, sits roughly seven kilometres below you, and in summer the snow shrinks to thin streaks in the gullies, leaving a dark, ash-coloured mountain.
Q39231.w: A lone snow-topped cone about 100 km south-west of Tokyo, with small lakes strung along its northern foot.
f: The five lakes around Fuji's northern foot formed where old lava flows dammed the valleys.
The 1707 eruption blew out a side crater on the south-east flank that breaks the cone's symmetry.
Fuji became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2013 — as a cultural site, not a natural one.

q.q: How many lakes make up the famous group at Fuji's northern foot?

Q513.t: The world's highest point, only about 2 km below you
Q513.s: Everest rarely looks tallest from the air: it hides among giant neighbours, a dark pyramid often trailing a plume of snow blown east by the jet stream. Its summit, 8,848 m, is only about two kilometres below cruising height. The rock at the very top is limestone that formed on an ancient sea floor and was lifted as India pushed into Asia.
Q513.w: A dark three-sided pyramid, often with a snow plume, rising above the glaciers on the Nepal–Tibet border.
f: Tibetans call it Chomolungma; in Nepal it is Sagarmatha.
Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary first reached the summit on 29 May 1953.
The English name, adopted in 1865, honours George Everest, a British surveyor-general of India.

q.q: Who reached the summit of Everest with Tenzing Norgay in 1953?

Q43512.t: Earth's second summit, a pyramid of the Karakoram
Q43512.s: The name K2 is just a surveyor's label — peak 2 on a Karakoram list drawn up in 1856, when no widely used local name was found. It is the second-highest mountain on Earth, 8,611 m, a steep, almost perfect pyramid ringed by rivers of ice. Look for a sharp summit at the head of a long glacier, far from any road or town.
Q43512.w: A lone sharp pyramid at the head of broad glacier tongues, on the border crest of the Karakoram.
f: The Italians Lino Lacedelli and Achille Compagnoni made the first ascent in 1954.
The first winter ascent came only in January 2021, by a team of Nepali climbers.
Its pyramid rises more than 3,000 m above the glaciers at its foot.

q.q: What does the 'K' in K2 stand for?

Q1374.t: The Alps' sharpest tooth, facing all four compass points
Q1374.s: Even from cruise height the Matterhorn looks carved: a hooked pyramid whose four faces point almost exactly north, south, east and west. It stands on the Swiss–Italian border above Zermatt, 4,478 m high and roughly six and a half kilometres below you. On a sunny morning its east face is lit while the north face stays in shadow, so the peak looks sliced in two.
Q1374.w: A lone, hooked rock pyramid among glaciers, west of the big Monte Rosa massif on the Swiss–Italian border.
f: Edward Whymper's party made the first ascent on 14 July 1865.
Italians call it Monte Cervino; in French it is Mont Cervin.
A summit ridge about 100 m long links two tops, a Swiss one and an Italian one.

q.q: From which Swiss village is the Matterhorn most often climbed?

ne-pk-1159105947.t: The volcano that buried Pompeii, still watching Naples
ne-pk-1159105947.s: Look for a cone inside a broken ring: Vesuvius grew within the collapsed crater of an older volcano, Monte Somma, whose ridge wraps around its north side. Naples spreads right up to its lower slopes, a dense grey carpet along the bay. On a clear day the summit crater, 1,281 m high, shows as a dark hole. Vesuvius has been quiet since 1944, but it is watched around the clock.
ne-pk-1159105947.w: A dark two-humped volcano on the Bay of Naples, with the city spread along the shore to its north-west.
f: In AD 79 its ash buried Pompeii and Herculaneum, preserving the Roman towns for archaeologists.
It is the only volcano on mainland Europe to have erupted in the last hundred years.
Its observatory, founded in 1841, is the oldest volcano observatory in the world.

q.q: Which Roman town, buried in AD 79, lies at the foot of Vesuvius?

Q583.t: Western Europe's highest dome, white all year
Q583.s: Mont Blanc is less a spike than a huge white shoulder: a broad dome of ice on a massif shared by France, Italy and Switzerland. At about 4,807 m it is the highest point of the Alps, yet still more than six kilometres below you. On its north side long glaciers pour down toward the valley of Chamonix; on the Italian side the walls drop steeply to Courmayeur.
Q583.w: A broad, rounded white dome above deep valleys, with long glacier tongues reaching toward Chamonix on its north-west side.
f: Jacques Balmat and Michel-Gabriel Paccard first reached the summit in 1786.
The summit is a cap of ice, and its height shifts by a metre or two from year to year.
The Mont Blanc road tunnel, 11.6 km long, runs beneath the massif between France and Italy.

q.q: In which year was Mont Blanc first climbed?

ne-pk-1159107423.t: Europe's restless giant, often trailing a plume
ne-pk-1159107423.s: Etna is the dark giant of eastern Sicily, a broad volcano whose summit, about 3,300 m high, often smokes. Its lower slopes are green with orchards and vineyards, the upper ones black with fresh lava, and in winter snow lies over both. Look for a thin plume drifting downwind: Etna erupts so often that its height changes every few years.
ne-pk-1159107423.w: A vast dark cone above Sicily's east coast, north of Catania, often with a steam plume and snow on top.
f: Etna covers about 1,200 km², and its base is roughly 140 km around.
It is the highest active volcano in Europe outside the Caucasus.
Etna became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2013.

q.q: Which city lies at the southern foot of Etna?

ne-gl-antarctic-ice-sheet.t: Most of the world's ice, on one frozen continent
ne-gl-antarctic-ice-sheet.s: If your route crosses Antarctica, the whiteness below is not snow on land but ice kilometres thick. The Antarctic Ice Sheet covers about 14 million km² and holds roughly 90% of all the ice on Earth. Its surface is so smooth and bright that the horizon can vanish; only nunataks — rocky peaks poking through the ice — break the white.
ne-gl-antarctic-ice-sheet.w: An endless white surface with faint wind ripples; dark rock shows only near the coast and along mountain ranges.
f: If it all melted, global sea level would rise by about 58 metres.
The ice is about two kilometres thick on average.
Its weight has pressed the bedrock beneath it down by hundreds of metres.

q.q: Roughly what share of Earth's ice lies in the Antarctic Ice Sheet?

ne-gl-greenland-ice-sheet.t: A 3-kilometre-thick lid on the world's largest island
ne-gl-greenland-ice-sheet.s: Crossing the North Atlantic, many flights pass over this white desert. The ice sheet covers about 80% of Greenland, some 1.7 million km², and rises into a dome more than 3,000 m high. Near the coast it breaks into crevassed outlet glaciers that snake down to fjords full of icebergs; in summer, bright blue meltwater lakes dot its western edge.
ne-gl-greenland-ice-sheet.w: Flat white expanse inland; at the edges, dark mountains, glacier tongues and fjords speckled with icebergs.
f: If the whole ice sheet melted, sea level would rise by roughly 7 metres.
Its weight has pushed the bedrock in the centre of Greenland below sea level.
Ice cores drilled through it hold a climate record reaching back more than 100,000 years.

q.q: How much would sea level rise if Greenland's ice sheet melted?

Q1001294.t: The coldest high desert on the planet
Q1001294.s: Around the South Pole the ice rises into a vast, gently sloping plateau, mostly around 3,000 m high and as flat as a frozen sea. It is a true desert: each year the snowfall adds up to only a few centimetres of water. Vostok Station, on this plateau, recorded −89.2 °C in 1983 — the lowest air temperature ever measured at the Earth's surface.
Q1001294.w: A featureless white plain to the horizon, scored only by long wind-carved snow ridges called sastrugi.
f: The South Pole itself lies on the plateau, about 2,835 m above sea level.
Antarctica's fierce coastal winds start here, as heavy cold air slides off the plateau toward the sea.
Its cold, dry, still air makes it one of the best places on Earth for telescopes.

q.q: What temperature did Vostok Station record in 1983?

Q165440.t: The white mountain that once topped the world's list
Q165440.s: Dhaulagiri means 'white mountain' in Sanskrit, and from the air it earns the name: a massive snowy wall rising straight out of central Nepal. Its main summit, about 8,170 m, is the seventh-highest on Earth. Just east of it the Kali Gandaki river cuts through the Himalaya between Dhaulagiri and Annapurna, carving one of the deepest valleys on the planet.
Q165440.w: A huge snowy massif west of the deep Kali Gandaki gorge, with Annapurna's white ridges on the other side.
f: After surveys in 1808 it was believed for some 30 years to be the highest mountain in the world.
A Swiss-Austrian expedition made the first ascent in 1960.
The Kali Gandaki gorge beside it was for centuries a trade route between Tibet and India.

q.q: Which river gorge separates Dhaulagiri from Annapurna?

Q130736.t: The 'naked mountain' at the western end of the Himalaya
Q130736.s: Nanga Parbat stands apart: the westernmost 8,000-metre peak of the Himalaya, with the Indus curving around its foot. Its name means 'naked mountain', perhaps for walls too steep to hold snow. The Rupal Face on its south side rises about 4,600 m from valley to summit, one of the tallest mountain walls on Earth. The top, 8,125 m, is less than three kilometres below you.
Q130736.w: An isolated giant massif south of a bend in the Indus, with a sheer southern wall and glaciers spilling north.
f: Hermann Buhl made the first ascent in 1953, reaching the summit alone.
It is the ninth-highest mountain on Earth.
The Indus flows past its northern flank at around 1,100 m — seven kilometres below the summit.

q.q: What does the name Nanga Parbat mean?

Q82019.t: Five treasures of snow above Sikkim and Nepal
Q82019.s: Kangchenjunga is not one summit but a crowded crown of them, five main tops on a single massif. At 8,586 m it is the third-highest mountain on Earth, and until the 1850s it was thought to be the highest. Look for a broad white wall towering over the green hills of Darjeeling and Sikkim; at sunrise its snow turns pink long before the valleys wake.
Q82019.w: A massive white massif rising above green foothills, north of Darjeeling on the Nepal–India border.
f: Its name is usually translated from Tibetan as 'Five Treasures of the Snow'.
The first climbers, in 1955, stopped just short of the top out of respect for local beliefs.
From the hill town of Darjeeling, about 75 km away, it fills the northern horizon.

q.q: Where does Kangchenjunga rank among the world's highest mountains?

Q604846.t: A red tableland of some of Earth's oldest rock
Q604846.s: For hours on a flight across Australia the ground barely changes: rust-red sand, pale salt lakes and dark scrub, a few hundred metres above sea level. This is the Western Plateau, spread over most of the western two-thirds of the continent. Its bedrock is among the oldest on Earth, and the deserts on top — the Gibson, the Great Sandy, the Great Victoria — are combed with long dune lines.
Q604846.w: Endless red and ochre ground streaked with parallel dunes and dotted with white salt lakes that shine like mirrors.
f: Zircon crystals from the Jack Hills in Western Australia are about 4.4 billion years old, the oldest known pieces of Earth.
Its dunes often run in parallel lines for tens of kilometres, aligned with the prevailing winds.
Salt lakes such as Lake Carnegie hold water only after rare heavy rains.

q.q: What record do zircons from Western Australia's Jack Hills hold?

Q179842.t: The roof of the world, averaging over 4,500 m
Q179842.s: Below you lies the highest large plateau on Earth, averaging more than 4,500 m and covering about 2.5 million km². From cruise it looks like another planet: brown and ochre plains, turquoise lakes with salt-white shores, snowy ranges ruled across it. Asia's great rivers — the Yangtze, Yellow, Mekong, Indus and Brahmaputra among them — begin up here.
Q179842.w: Bare brown highland with scattered turquoise lakes and white ridges; the Himalaya forms its sharp southern rim.
f: It holds so much glacier ice that it is often called the Third Pole.
Lhasa, in the south of the plateau, lies at about 3,650 m.
The plateau is still rising as India keeps pushing north into Asia.

q.q: Which nickname does the Tibetan Plateau get for its glaciers?

ne-gl-flade-isblink.t: Greenland's biggest ice cap that stands on its own
ne-gl-flade-isblink.s: Near Greenland's north-eastern tip a separate dome of ice sits apart from the main ice sheet: Flade Isblink, some 8,000 km² of white. Its Danish name means roughly 'flat iceblink' — the glow that ice casts on low clouds. The ice is up to about 600 m thick, and parts of its edge surge forward from time to time, pushing ice out to sea.
ne-gl-flade-isblink.w: A smooth, low white dome on a peninsula of north-east Greenland, cut off from the main ice sheet by bare land.
f: It is the largest ice cap in Greenland that is not joined to the main ice sheet.
Station Nord, the only inhabited place in the area, lies just to its north-west.
The whole area is part of Northeast Greenland National Park, the largest national park in the world.

q.q: What does the word 'iceblink' describe?
q.a: The glow of ice on clouds

Q163758.t: The highest point of the frozen continent
Q163758.s: Vinson is the summit of Antarctica, 4,892 m, a long snowy massif in the Sentinel Range of the Ellsworth Mountains, some 1,300 km from the South Pole. US Navy aircraft spotted it in 1958, and climbers first reached the top in 1966. From above the range looks like a spine of dark rock and ice breaking out of the ice sheet, with glaciers flowing away on both sides.
Q163758.w: A long, dark rock-and-ice ridge rising sharply above the flat ice sheet in the Ellsworth Mountains.
f: It is named after Carl Vinson, a US congressman who backed Antarctic exploration.
An American expedition made the first ascent in December 1966.
Climbers fly in to a blue-ice runway at Union Glacier to start their approach.

q.q: In which mountains does Vinson Massif rise?

Q1537198.t: Twin summits of ice above Ladakh's Suru valley
Q1537198.s: Nun and its twin, Kun, form the Nun Kun massif, a knot of ice in the western Himalaya of Ladakh. Nun is the higher of the pair at 7,135 m, only about four kilometres below you. Between the two tops lies a snowy plateau some 4 km long, and from above it looks like a white saddle slung between two peaks. Glaciers pour off both sides toward the Suru valley.
Q1537198.w: Two white summits joined by a snowy plateau, with long glaciers running down to a green valley at their foot.
f: Nun was first climbed in 1953 by Claude Kogan and Pierre Vittoz of a French–Swiss expedition.
Kun, the lower twin, is a little over 7,000 m high.
The Parkachik Glacier flows off the massif almost down to the road in the Suru valley.

q.q: What is the name of Nun's twin summit?

Q811064.t: The crown of the Karakoram's jagged western wall
Q811064.s: Batura Sar tops a long, serrated wall of ice in the far west of the Karakoram, the Batura Muztagh. At 7,795 m it is the highest point of that wall, yet it is little known outside climbing circles. Below it lies one of the longest glaciers outside the polar regions, the Batura: a grey-and-white river of ice that ends right beside the Karakoram Highway in the Hunza valley.
Q811064.w: A long, serrated ice ridge north-west of the Hunza valley, with a broad glacier sliding east toward the river.
f: The Batura Glacier is about 57 km long.
Muztagh means 'ice mountain' in Turkic languages.
The Karakoram Highway, one of the highest paved roads in the world, passes the glacier's snout.

q.q: Which famous road passes the snout of the Batura Glacier?

Q6654097.t: The Kunlun's highest peak, lost in a cold desert
Q6654097.s: This is one of the emptiest corners of Asia. Liushi Shan, also called the Kunlun Goddess, is the highest peak of the Kunlun Mountains at 7,167 m, rising from bleak high desert on the border of Tibet and Xinjiang. From above, look for a cluster of white ice domes and glaciers in a sea of brown, wind-scoured ridges.
Q6654097.w: A cluster of white ice domes on the northern edge of the Tibetan Plateau, surrounded by bare brown ridges.
f: A Japanese university team made the first ascent in 1986.
In Chinese it is also known as Kunlun Nüshen Feng, 'Kunlun Goddess Peak'.
The Keriya River rises in this part of the Kunlun, flows north and vanishes into the Taklamakan Desert.

q.q: Liushi Shan is the highest peak of which mountain system?

Q1050238.t: Where the Himalaya ends and a great river turns
Q1050238.s: Namcha Barwa marks the eastern end of the Himalaya, beside one of the strangest river bends on Earth: the Yarlung Tsangpo, flowing east across Tibet, swings around the mountain and plunges south through a gorge far deeper than the Grand Canyon. The peak is 7,782 m high, a steep white pyramid above dark, forested valleys, often wrapped in monsoon cloud.
Q1050238.w: A steep white peak where the brown Tibetan plateau gives way to green, cloudy gorges; a river loops around its foot.
f: It was the highest unclimbed peak in the world until a Chinese–Japanese team reached the top in 1992.
Gyala Peri, 7,294 m, rises only about 20 km away on the other side of the gorge.
Downstream from the gorge, the Yarlung Tsangpo becomes the Brahmaputra.

q.q: Which river bends sharply around Namcha Barwa?

Q26794321.t: A goddess inside a fortress of peaks
Q26794321.s: Nanda Devi rises inside a natural fortress: a ring of mountains, broken only by a narrow gorge, encloses the high glacial basin known as the Sanctuary. The double-topped peak, 7,817 m, is the highest mountain lying entirely within India and is revered as the goddess Nanda. From above, look for the ring itself — a near-circle of white summits around a bowl of ice.
Q26794321.w: A double-topped white peak inside a near-circle of snowy summits, in the Himalaya west of the Nepal border.
f: Bill Tilman and Noel Odell made the first ascent in 1936.
Eric Shipton and Tilman were the first to force a way up the Rishi Ganga gorge into the Sanctuary, in 1934.
Nanda Devi National Park and the nearby Valley of Flowers form a UNESCO World Heritage site.

q.q: What is the ring-walled basin around Nanda Devi called?

Q41413.t: The Pamirs' high point, a peak of three names
Q41413.s: For decades this was the highest point of the Soviet Union, first as Stalin Peak, then as Communism Peak. Since 1998 it has carried the name of Ismoil Somoni, a Samanid ruler of the 9th and 10th centuries. The summit, 7,495 m, crowns a massive white wall in the heart of the Pamirs, close to the Fedchenko Glacier, one of the great ice rivers of Asia.
Q41413.w: A massive white peak at a junction of ridges, west of the long, straight Fedchenko Glacier in the high Pamirs.
f: Yevgeny Abalakov made the first ascent in 1933.
The Fedchenko Glacier nearby is about 77 km long, the longest outside the polar regions.
Tajikistan's currency, the somoni, is named after the same ruler.

q.q: What was the peak called from 1962 to 1998?

Q1537157.s: Gongga, also known as Minya Konka, stands where the Tibetan highlands drop toward the Sichuan Basin. At 7,556 m it is the highest peak in Sichuan and the easternmost 7,000-metre summit on Earth. Look for a sharp white pyramid ringed by glaciers, with the deep Dadu River valley to the east — more than six kilometres of relief in a short distance.
Q1537157.w: A sharp white pyramid with a skirt of glaciers, west of the deep Dadu River gorge in western Sichuan.
f: An American team made the first ascent in 1932.
The Hailuogou Glacier on its eastern side reaches down into forest below 3,000 m.
Gongga is the highest point of the Daxue Shan, the 'Great Snowy Mountains'.

q.q: Which glacier descends from Gongga's east side into forest?

Q6362901.t: A cloud-wrapped giant of the eastern Himalaya
Q6362901.s: East of Bhutan the Himalaya grows wilder and wetter, and Kangto is one of its tallest summits, just over 7,000 m. It sits on the main crest, where the dry Tibetan uplands meet steep valleys draining south toward the Brahmaputra plains of Assam. Thick forest climbs its lower flanks, and monsoon cloud hides the peak for much of the summer, so a clear view is a rare prize.
Q6362901.w: A white summit on the Himalayan crest north of the Brahmaputra plains, between dry brown highlands and forested valleys.
f: Kangto remained unclimbed for decades; the first recorded ascent came only in 2025.
Its southern valleys drain toward the Kameng River, a tributary of the Brahmaputra.
The eastern Himalaya receives far more monsoon rain than the ranges around Everest.

q.q: Toward which great river do Kangto's southern valleys drain?

Q1109058.t: A mountain god guarding a turquoise lake
Q1109058.s: Nyenchen Tanglha is the highest peak of a long range running across central Tibet north-west of Lhasa. Look for its white summit, 7,162 m, just south-east of Namtso, a huge salt lake of startling turquoise. In Tibetan tradition the mountain is a protector deity, and he and the lake are often spoken of as a couple.
Q1109058.w: A white ridge just south-east of a large turquoise lake, Namtso, on the brown plateau north-west of Lhasa.
f: Namtso, at its foot, lies about 4,700 m above sea level.
The lake covers nearly 2,000 km², one of the largest in Tibet.
The railway and highway from Qinghai to Lhasa run along the range's southern foot.

q.q: Which lake lies at the foot of Nyenchen Tanglha?

Q1560829.t: The 'great ice mountain' of Tibet's empty north
Q1560829.s: Ulugh Muztagh means 'great ice mountain' in Uyghur, and it rules one of the loneliest places on Earth: the high, cold uplands on the border of Tibet and Xinjiang, far from any town. The summit, 6,973 m, crowns a compact knot of ice-covered ridges. Around it the ground is pale brown desert, dotted with salt lakes that flash white and blue.
Q1560829.w: A compact cluster of white summits and glaciers rising from pale brown desert and scattered salt lakes.
f: After his journey of 1895, the explorer George Littledale guessed it was over 7,700 m high.
A Chinese–American expedition made the first ascent in 1985 and measured its true height.
Its meltwater drains into closed basins and never reaches the sea.

q.q: What does the name Ulugh Muztagh mean?

Q229107.t: A sacred rock pyramid that no one has climbed
Q229107.s: Kailash looks almost designed: a lone, four-sided dome of dark rock streaked with snow, standing apart in the far west of Tibet. It is sacred to Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and followers of Bon, and climbing it is not permitted. Pilgrims instead walk around it, a circuit of about 52 km. Just to the south, two big lakes lie side by side: Manasarovar and Rakshastal.
Q229107.w: A lone snow-streaked rock dome north of two large lakes lying side by side on the brown plateau.
f: The Indus, Sutlej, Brahmaputra and Karnali all rise within about 100 km of it.
Lake Manasarovar, at about 4,590 m, is fresh, while its neighbour Rakshastal is salty.
The pilgrim circuit crosses a pass at about 5,600 m.

q.q: Which sacred freshwater lake lies just south of Mount Kailash?

Q207132.t: King of the Hindu Kush, above the Chitral valley
Q207132.s: Tirich Mir is the highest mountain of the Hindu Kush, 7,708 m, and it rules the valley of Chitral in northern Pakistan. From cruise height it looks like a great snowy tent with long ridges, standing north of the green thread of the Chitral river. Beyond it the land runs north toward Afghanistan's Wakhan Corridor, a narrow strip squeezed between high ranges.
Q207132.w: A massive snowy peak with long ridges, north of the town of Chitral and close to the Afghan border.
f: A Norwegian expedition made the first ascent in 1950.
The Hindu Kush stretches about 800 km from northern Pakistan into central Afghanistan.
The town of Chitral lies about 40 km to its south.

q.q: Tirich Mir is the highest peak of which range?

Q332762.s: Jengish Chokusu, long known as Victory Peak, is the highest point of the Tian Shan, 7,439 m, on the border of Kyrgyzstan and China. No mountain over 7,000 m stands farther north. Look for a long, heavy ridge of ice rather than a spike; just to its north rises the sharper pyramid of Khan Tengri, whose marble summit glows pink at sunset.
Q332762.w: A long, heavy white ridge on the Kyrgyz–Chinese border, with the sharp pyramid of Khan Tengri about 16 km north.
f: It was recognised as the Tian Shan's highest peak only in the 1940s; Khan Tengri had long been thought higher.
The South Inylchek Glacier at its foot is about 60 km long.
Jengish Chokusu is Kyrgyz for 'Victory Peak'.

q.q: Which sharp peak rises just north of Jengish Chokusu?

Q271700.t: Afghanistan's highest summit, on the Hindu Kush crest
Q271700.s: Noshaq is the highest point of Afghanistan and the second-highest mountain of the Hindu Kush, 7,492 m, standing right on the border with Pakistan. From above it shows as a broad white massif with several summits in a row, a short way north of Tirich Mir. Its northern glaciers drain into the Wakhan valley, where the rivers gather that later form the Amu Darya.
Q271700.w: A broad white massif with a row of summits on the Afghan–Pakistani border, just north of Tirich Mir.
f: A Japanese expedition made the first ascent in 1960.
It stands just south of the Wakhan Corridor, a thin arm of Afghanistan reaching east to China.

q.q: Noshaq is the highest point of which country?

Q8536063.t: The top of the Transhimalaya, Tibet's second wall
Q8536063.s: North of the great Himalayan wall runs a second, lesser-known chain: the Transhimalaya, or Gangdise. Its highest summit is Lunpo Gangri, 7,095 m, an ice-capped massif in south-western Tibet. Look for a line of white peaks rising from brown uplands, with the upper Yarlung Tsangpo — the future Brahmaputra — winding through a broad valley to the south.
Q8536063.w: An ice-capped massif north of the broad Yarlung Tsangpo valley, part of a white chain parallel to the Himalaya.
f: Mount Kailash belongs to the same Gangdise range, about 300 km to the west.
The Swedish explorer Sven Hedin named the Transhimalaya after travelling through it in 1906–1908.

q.q: Which explorer gave the Transhimalaya its name?

ne-pk-1159105819.t: The ice giant above the Karakoram Highway
ne-pk-1159105819.s: Kongur Tagh, 7,649 m, is a massive dome of ice at the western edge of the Tarim Basin, not far from Kashgar. Its neighbour to the south, Muztagh Ata, is rounder and more famous, but Kongur is higher. Between the two the Karakoram Highway runs past Karakul Lake, a blue mirror at about 3,600 m that reflects both peaks on calm days.
ne-pk-1159105819.w: A huge ice massif east of the Karakoram Highway, with the rounder Muztagh Ata to the south and a small blue lake between.
f: A British team including Chris Bonington made the first ascent in 1981.
Kashgar, the old Silk Road oasis, lies roughly 100 km to the north-east.
Its summit rises more than 6,000 m above the floor of the Tarim Basin.

q.q: Which famous peak stands just south of Kongur Tagh?

Q1322521.t: The northern sentinel of Tibet's great gorge
Q1322521.s: Gyala Peri and Namcha Barwa face each other across the Yarlung Tsangpo, only about 20 km apart. Between them the river squeezes through a gorge of extraordinary depth before turning south toward India. Gyala Peri, 7,294 m, is the northern guard: a white dome above slopes so wet and steep that dense forest climbs far up its sides.
Q1322521.w: A white dome on the north side of a tight river bend, facing the higher Namcha Barwa across a dark gorge.
f: Between Gyala Peri and Namcha Barwa the gorge is more than 5,000 m deep.
The botanist Frank Kingdon-Ward explored the gorge in 1924 in search of new plants.

q.q: Which peak faces Gyala Peri across the Yarlung Tsangpo gorge?

Q219986.t: The highest mountain no one has climbed
Q219986.s: Gangkhar Puensum, 7,570 m, is the highest point of Bhutan and very likely the highest unclimbed mountain on Earth. Attempts in the 1980s failed, and since 1994 Bhutan has banned climbing peaks over 6,000 m out of respect for the belief that mountains are home to spirits. Look for a broad white summit on the northern border, above deep, forested valleys.
Q219986.w: A broad white summit on Bhutan's northern border with Tibet, above deep, green, forested valleys.
f: Its name is usually translated as 'White Peak of the Three Spiritual Brothers'.
Since 2003 Bhutan has banned mountaineering altogether.
In 1999 a Japanese team climbed a neighbouring summit, Liankang Kangri, from the Tibetan side.

q.q: Since which year has Bhutan banned climbing peaks over 6,000 m?

Q43105.t: A double-humped volcano crowning the Caucasus
Q43105.s: Elbrus stands a little north of the main Caucasus ridge, and from the air its shape gives it away: two rounded white domes, the remains of a dormant volcano, joined by a saddle. The western summit, 5,642 m, is the highest point in Russia and is often counted as the top of Europe. Its ice cap feeds more than twenty glaciers that radiate outward like the spokes of a wheel.
Q43105.w: Two rounded snow domes side by side, standing just north of the jagged main Caucasus ridge.
f: The eastern summit, 5,621 m, is only about 20 m lower than the western one.
Its last eruption is thought to have happened around AD 50.
Cable cars carry visitors from the Baksan valley up to about 3,800 m on its southern slope.

q.q: How many main summits does Elbrus have?

Q130018.t: North America's summit, rising from near sea level
Q130018.s: Denali is the highest mountain in North America, about 6,200 m, and one of the bulkiest on Earth. It rises from lowlands only about 600 m above sea level, so its climb from base to summit — some 5,500 m — is greater than Everest's. Look for a huge white mass with long glaciers flowing out of it, dwarfing the rest of the Alaska Range.
Q130018.w: An enormous white massif towering over the Alaska Range, about 210 km north of Anchorage.
f: Its name means 'the high one' in the Koyukon Athabaskan language.
An expedition led by Hudson Stuck and Harry Karstens made the first ascent in 1913.
The Kahiltna Glacier on its south side is about 70 km long, the longest in the Alaska Range.

q.q: What does 'Denali' mean in the Koyukon language?

Q235539.t: The Lower 48's highest summit, above a desert valley
Q235539.s: Mount Whitney is the highest point of the contiguous United States, 4,421 m, on the sharp eastern edge of the Sierra Nevada. Its granite wall drops steeply to the dry Owens Valley, more than three kilometres below. Only about 135 km to the south-east lies Badwater Basin in Death Valley, the lowest point in North America — the continent's high and low points almost within sight of each other.
Q235539.w: A saw-toothed granite crest above the brown Owens Valley, directly west of the small town of Lone Pine.
f: Badwater Basin, 86 m below sea level, lies only about 135 km away.
Three fishermen from Lone Pine first reached the summit in 1873.
It is named after Josiah Whitney, head of the California Geological Survey.

q.q: Which low point lies about 135 km from Mount Whitney?

Q178167.t: Australia's rooftop, a gentle granite hump
Q178167.s: Mount Kosciuszko is the highest mountain on mainland Australia, yet at 2,228 m it is a rounded summit that walkers reach from the top of a chairlift. From above, the Snowy Mountains look like a rumpled plateau, white for a few months each winter and grey-green the rest of the year. Look for the long blue arms of Lake Jindabyne and other reservoirs winding through the valleys below.
Q178167.w: A rounded, often snowy plateau south-west of Canberra, with long blue reservoirs winding through the valleys.
f: The explorer Paweł Strzelecki named it in 1840 after the Polish patriot Tadeusz Kościuszko.
The Snowy Mountains Scheme, built from 1949 to 1974, sends the mountains' water through tunnels to power stations and farms.
Mainland Australia's only glacial lakes, including Blue Lake, lie near its summit.

q.q: Who was Mount Kosciuszko named after?

Q39739.t: The highest peak on Earth outside Asia
Q39739.s: Aconcagua is the tallest mountain outside Asia, 6,959 m, and the summit of both the Western and Southern hemispheres. It rises in Argentina just east of the Chilean border, a huge brown-and-white massif rather than a slender spike. On flights between Santiago and Mendoza it often looms off the wing, barely four kilometres below you.
Q39739.w: A massive white-topped peak above the Andes' dry brown ridges, just north of the route between Santiago and Mendoza.
f: Matthias Zurbriggen made the first recorded ascent in 1897.
Its normal route needs no technical climbing, only stamina and careful acclimatisation.
The name is often traced to Quechua words meaning 'stone sentinel', though its origin is debated.

q.q: Aconcagua is the highest peak outside which continent?

ne-pk-1159108759.t: A lonely summit above Venezuela's rainforest
ne-pk-1159108759.s: Deep in Venezuela's Amazonas state, far from any road, Cerro La Raya rises to about 2,000 m above an unbroken green sea of forest. It belongs to the Guiana Highlands, a region of ancient sandstone mountains and flat-topped tepuis. Look for dark ridges poking through the canopy, often wrapped in afternoon cloud, with brown rivers winding away toward the Orinoco.
ne-pk-1159108759.w: Forested ridges and cloud-capped heights rising from unbroken rainforest, with brown rivers winding west toward the Orinoco.
f: Venezuela's Amazonas state is larger than many European countries but very thinly populated.
In the same state the Casiquiare, a natural channel, links the Orinoco and Amazon river systems.
Nearby tepuis such as Cerro Autana have sheer walls rising straight out of the forest.

q.q: Which natural channel in Venezuela's Amazonas links the Orinoco and Amazon?

Q1108926.t: Copper country on the roof of central Africa
Q1108926.s: South-eastern DR Congo rises into the Katanga Plateau: high savanna and open woodland mostly over 1,000 m, crossed by the divide between Congo and Zambezi waters. Beneath it lie some of the richest copper and cobalt deposits on Earth. Look for enormous open-pit mines and tailings ponds — grey and turquoise scars — around the cities of Lubumbashi and Kolwezi.
Q1108926.w: Green-brown savanna and woodland dotted with grey open-pit mines and bright turquoise ponds near Kolwezi and Lubumbashi.
f: DR Congo produces around 70% of the world's cobalt, most of it from this region.
The Lualaba, the upper course of the Congo River, rises on the plateau.
The copper belt continues south across the border into Zambia's Copperbelt.

q.q: Which battery metal is mined heavily on the Katanga Plateau?

Q208807.t: Tabletop mountains rising from the rainforest
Q208807.s: Across northern South America, sheer-sided table mountains called tepuis rise from the rainforest like islands, their flat tops often lost in cloud. They are carved from sandstone laid down about 1.7 billion years ago, among the oldest sedimentary rocks on the continent. Look for dark, cliff-edged blocks above the green, and in the rainy season thin white threads of waterfalls dropping from their rims.
Q208807.w: Flat-topped, cliff-edged blocks of dark rock standing above unbroken rainforest, often capped with cloud.
f: Angel Falls, dropping 979 m from Auyán-tepui, is the highest uninterrupted waterfall in the world.
Mount Roraima, about 2,810 m, marks the meeting point of Venezuela, Brazil and Guyana.
Tepui is a Pemón word usually translated as 'house of the gods'.

q.q: Which record-breaking waterfall pours off a tepui here?

Q118899.t: The old stone heart of Brazil
Q118899.s: Much of eastern and central Brazil is a vast upland of ancient rock, worn into long flat-topped plateaus called chapadas with steep edges. Brasília was built on it in the late 1950s, at over 1,000 m. From the air look for red-earth tablelands, cerrado savanna in olive and gold, and huge green circles of irrigated farmland laid out like coins on a table.
Q118899.w: Flat-topped red tablelands with steep edges, olive-green savanna and neat green circles of centre-pivot irrigation.
f: The São Francisco, the longest river entirely within Brazil, flows north across the highlands for much of its course.
Brasília was inaugurated as the capital in 1960.
The cerrado savanna covering much of it is one of the most species-rich savannas on Earth.

q.q: Which is the longest river flowing entirely within Brazil?

Q155197.t: Taiga, rivers and old lava to the horizon
Q155197.s: Between the Yenisei and the Lena lies a vast raised upland, mostly 500 to 700 m high and cut by deep river valleys. Much of it is built from the Siberian Traps, lava that poured out about 250 million years ago. From cruise height it is endless larch taiga: dark green in summer, gold in autumn, and white under snow for most of the year.
Q155197.w: Endless dark taiga cut by winding rivers in deep valleys, with flat-topped uplands and, in autumn, golden larch.
f: The Siberian Traps eruptions are linked to the greatest mass extinction in Earth's history, about 252 million years ago.
In 1908 the Tunguska explosion flattened some 2,000 km² of forest on the plateau.
Permafrost underlies nearly all of it, in places hundreds of metres deep.

q.q: Which 1908 event flattened forest on the Central Siberian Plateau?

Q560198.t: Grassland under a huge sky, a kilometre up
Q560198.s: The Mongolian Plateau spreads across Mongolia and northern China at around 1,000 to 1,500 m: rolling steppe, bare hills and, to the south, the stony Gobi. Few places look so open from the air. Roads are faint tracks, rivers wander freely, and lakes shine like scattered coins. Ulaanbaatar, on the plateau at about 1,350 m, is the coldest national capital on Earth.
Q560198.w: Rolling green-brown steppe with few roads, meandering rivers and, to the south, pale stony desert.
f: Ulaanbaatar has the lowest average temperature of any national capital.
Lake Khövsgöl, in the north, holds about 70% of Mongolia's fresh water.
At the Flaming Cliffs in the Gobi, scientists found the first recognised dinosaur egg nests in 1923.

q.q: Which is the coldest national capital, on this plateau?

Q169966.t: India's tilted tableland of ancient lava
Q169966.s: The Deccan fills most of southern India, a triangular plateau raised along its western edge by the Western Ghats and tilted toward the east. So its great rivers — the Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri — rise near the Arabian Sea yet flow right across to the Bay of Bengal. Much of the north-west is built of Deccan Traps basalt, poured out as lava about 66 million years ago.
Q169966.w: A dry brown tableland of flat-topped hills, reservoirs and rivers draining east; much greener in the monsoon months.
f: Its name comes from the Sanskrit word dakshina, 'south'.
Hyderabad and Bengaluru both stand on the plateau, at about 500 and 900 m.
The Deccan Traps eruptions took place around the time the dinosaurs died out.

q.q: Where do most of the Deccan's great rivers flow?
q.a: East to the Bay of Bengal

Q1908889.t: Where the Amazon forest meets the fields
Q1908889.s: Mato Grosso means 'thick bush' in Portuguese, and this plateau sits in the heart of Brazil, where Amazon rainforest gives way to cerrado savanna. From the air it is a patchwork: huge rectangles of soy and maize, strips of forest along the rivers, and red dirt roads ruled straight for kilometres. Its rivers split two ways, north to the Amazon and south toward the Pantanal.
Q1908889.w: A vast chessboard of green and tan fields with ruler-straight roads, cut by dark lines of forest along rivers.
f: The Xingu and the rivers that form the Tapajós, big Amazon tributaries, rise on this plateau.
The Xingu Indigenous Park, founded in 1961, shows from above as a great block of forest ringed by farmland.
Mato Grosso state is Brazil's leading soybean producer.

q.q: What does 'Mato Grosso' mean in Portuguese?

Q7680307.t: A snowy ice dome above the Ross Sea coast
Q7680307.s: Talos Dome is a broad, gentle summit of the East Antarctic ice, about 2,300 m high, inland from the coast of northern Victoria Land. Unlike the bone-dry domes of the deep interior, it catches a good deal of snow from storms off the Ross Sea and the Southern Ocean. That leaves thick, readable yearly layers in its ice, and scientists have drilled deep into them.
Q7680307.w: A barely noticeable swell in the white ice sheet, with the dark peaks of Victoria Land between it and the coast.
f: A European ice-coring project, TALDICE, drilled more than 1,600 m into the dome in the 2000s.
Its ice core holds a climate record of roughly 250,000 years.

q.q: Which sea lies toward the coast from Talos Dome?

Q470049.t: An icy upland named on a 1939 flight
Q470049.s: American Highland is a high, ice-covered upland in East Antarctica, beside the vast valley of the Lambert Glacier. The American explorer Lincoln Ellsworth flew over it in 1939 and gave it its name. From above it is a smooth white slope crossed by faint ridges, falling toward the giant ice stream of the Lambert and the flat Amery Ice Shelf beyond.
Q470049.w: A smooth, faintly ridged white upland sloping toward a vast glacier valley and the flat Amery Ice Shelf.
f: The Lambert Glacier nearby is one of the largest glaciers on Earth, several hundred kilometres long.
Ellsworth's 1939 flight took off from his expedition ship, the Wyatt Earp.
The Amery Ice Shelf, fed by the Lambert, floats at the head of Prydz Bay.

q.q: Who named the American Highland after a flight in 1939?

Q5881339.t: Named for the pilot of the first flight across Antarctica
Q5881339.s: This broad ice plateau in West Antarctica carries the name of Herbert Hollick-Kenyon, who in 1935 flew Lincoln Ellsworth across the continent for the first time. The crossing took about two weeks, because they had to land on the open ice several times to wait out storms. Below you is an endless, gently rolling white expanse with hardly a rock in sight.
Q5881339.w: A featureless, gently rolling white plateau between the Ellsworth Mountains and the ranges of Marie Byrd Land.
f: The 1935 flight ran out of fuel short of the Bay of Whales, and the two men walked the last stretch.
Ellsworth named the plateau after his pilot.

q.q: What did Herbert Hollick-Kenyon do in 1935?

Q370807.t: A white upland named after an expedition backer
Q370807.s: The Rockefeller Plateau is a vast, ice-buried upland in West Antarctica, inland from the Ross Ice Shelf. Richard Byrd's expedition flew over it in 1934 and named it after John D. Rockefeller Jr., one of Byrd's sponsors. From above there is only smooth white ice to the horizon; the bedrock lies well over a kilometre down, much of it below sea level.
Q370807.w: Smooth white ice to the horizon, east of the flat Ross Ice Shelf, with no rock visible at all.
f: Much of the bedrock beneath West Antarctica's ice lies below sea level.
Byrd's base, Little America, stood on the Ross Ice Shelf to the west.

q.q: Whose expedition discovered and named the Rockefeller Plateau?

Q3045552.t: A year-round outpost on the ice, 3,200 m up
Q3045552.s: Dome C is one of the high summits of the East Antarctic ice, about 3,200 m above sea level, where France and Italy run Concordia, a station staffed all year. Winter temperatures here fall below −80 °C, and for months the sun never rises. An ice core drilled at Dome C holds a record of Earth's climate reaching back some 800,000 years.
Q3045552.w: A flat white summit of the ice sheet with nothing to mark it — the station is far too small to see.
f: The European EPICA project drilled 3,270 m of ice here, spanning about 800,000 years.
Space agencies study Concordia's winter crews to learn how people cope with isolation on long missions.
In 2025 the Beyond EPICA project reached ice over a million years old at nearby Little Dome C.

q.q: Which two countries run Concordia Station at Dome C?

Q593197.t: The highest summit of Antarctica's ice
Q593197.s: Dome A is the highest point of the Antarctic ice sheet, about 4,090 m above sea level, deep in East Antarctica. Under some three kilometres of ice lie the Gamburtsev Mountains, a range roughly the size of the Alps that no one has ever seen. China set up its Kunlun Station here in 2009, and satellites have found some of Earth's coldest surface temperatures nearby.
Q593197.w: An utterly flat white horizon; the summit of the ice rises so gently that you cannot pick it out.
f: Soviet scientists discovered the buried Gamburtsev Mountains in 1958 with seismic soundings.
Satellite readings on the ice ridge near Dome A have dropped below −90 °C.
A Chinese traverse team first reached Dome A in 2005.

q.q: What lies hidden beneath the ice at Dome A?

Q2007598.t: Japan's station on a summit of the ice
Q2007598.s: Dome Fuji, also called Dome F, is a high summit of the East Antarctic ice sheet, about 3,800 m up, far inland in Queen Maud Land. Japan opened a research station here in 1995 and drilled deep into the ice beneath it; the cores reach back roughly 700,000 years. Up here the air is so cold and still that temperatures below −79 °C have been recorded.
Q2007598.w: A broad white summit of the ice sheet, featureless to the horizon, far inland from the coast of Queen Maud Land.
f: Japanese expeditions named the dome after Mount Fuji.
Only a few centimetres of water a year fall here as snow, making it one of the driest places on Earth.
The ice ridge between Dome Fuji and Dome A holds some of the coldest surface temperatures ever measured.

q.q: Which country runs the research station at Dome Fuji?

ne-gl-academy-of-sciences-ice-cap.t: Russia's largest ice cap, a round lid on an Arctic island
ne-gl-academy-of-sciences-ice-cap.s: Near the top of Severnaya Zemlya, an almost perfectly round dome of ice covers most of Komsomolets Island. The Academy of Sciences Ice Cap is about 80 km across and some 5,500 km² in area, the largest single ice mass in Russia. From above it looks like a white lid dropped on a dark sea, its edges crumbling into ice cliffs and drifting floes.
ne-gl-academy-of-sciences-ice-cap.w: A round, smooth white dome filling most of an island, with ice cliffs along its edges and sea ice around.
f: Severnaya Zemlya was one of the last archipelagos on Earth to be discovered, in 1913.
Georgy Ushakov and Nikolay Urvantsev first mapped the islands in 1930–1932, travelling by dog sled.
The ice is hundreds of metres thick at the centre of the dome.

q.q: On which island does the Academy of Sciences Ice Cap lie?

ne-gl-agassiz-ice-cap.t: An Arctic ice cap named for the Ice Age's discoverer
ne-gl-agassiz-ice-cap.s: On northern Ellesmere Island, Canada's northernmost, the Agassiz Ice Cap spreads over the high interior like poured icing. It carries the name of Louis Agassiz, the Swiss-born scientist who in the 1830s argued that great ice sheets had once covered much of the northern world. Look for a smooth white dome cut at its edges by dark rock ridges and glacier tongues sliding toward the fjords.
ne-gl-agassiz-ice-cap.w: A smooth white dome over Ellesmere's high interior, fringed by dark rock ridges and glacier tongues heading for the fjords.
f: Ice cores drilled here since the 1970s record Arctic temperatures over thousands of years.
Ellesmere Island is the tenth-largest island in the world.

q.q: Louis Agassiz is famous for which idea?

ne-gl-asgardfonna.t: An ice plateau named after the home of the Norse gods
ne-gl-asgardfonna.s: In the north-east of Spitsbergen, between two long fjords, lies Åsgardfonna, a plateau of ice some 1,200 km² in area. Its name comes from Åsgard, the home of the gods in Norse myth, and neighbouring ice fields borrow names from the same stories. From above it is a high white tableland, with dark ridges and valley glaciers spilling off its sides.
ne-gl-asgardfonna.w: A high white ice plateau between two long fjords, Wijdefjorden to the west and Lomfjorden to the east.
f: Nearby ice fields are called Valhallfonna and Balderfonna, also after Norse mythology.
Wijdefjorden, on its western side, is Svalbard's longest fjord, over 100 km long.

q.q: In Norse myth, what is Åsgard?

ne-gl-barnes-ice-cap.t: The last surviving piece of the great Ice Age sheet
ne-gl-barnes-ice-cap.s: In the middle of Baffin Island lies a smooth white dome some 150 km long, and it is older than it looks. The Barnes Ice Cap is the last remnant of the Laurentide Ice Sheet, which buried most of Canada during the last ice age, and its deepest layers still hold ice from that time. Around it the land is brown tundra scattered with thousands of lakes.
ne-gl-barnes-ice-cap.w: A long, smooth white dome in the centre of Baffin Island, surrounded by brown tundra freckled with lakes.
f: It covers about 6,000 km².
Scientists expect it to disappear within a few centuries as the Arctic warms.
Baffin Island is the fifth-largest island in the world.

q.q: The Barnes Ice Cap is a remnant of which ice sheet?

ne-gl-bering-glacier.t: North America's longest glacier, a river of ice
ne-gl-bering-glacier.s: Flying along the Gulf of Alaska, look for a vast lobe of ice spreading onto the coastal plain: the Bering Glacier, roughly 190 km long, the longest and largest glacier in North America. It flows from the Bagley Icefield in the Chugach and Saint Elias mountains. Dark stripes of rock debris ripple across its surface, bent into waves by past surges.
ne-gl-bering-glacier.w: A huge ice lobe spilling onto the coastal plain east of the Copper River delta, streaked with dark, wavy lines.
f: It is named after the explorer Vitus Bering and has surged forward several times in the past century.
At its snout lies Vitus Lake, crowded with floating icebergs.

q.q: Which icefield feeds the Bering Glacier?

ne-gl-brasvellbreen.t: The ice wall that leapt 20 km in two years
ne-gl-brasvellbreen.s: On Nordaustlandet, Svalbard's second-largest island, the Austfonna ice cap ends in a long, low cliff, and Bråsvellbreen is its biggest outlet. In 1936–38 it surged forward by up to 20 km along a 30 km front, one of the largest glacier surges ever recorded. In summer, meltwater pours off the ice cliff in dozens of waterfalls straight into the sea.
ne-gl-brasvellbreen.w: A long, low ice cliff running along the sea, the edge of a huge white ice cap on Svalbard's second-largest island.
f: Its Norwegian name means roughly 'sudden swell', after that surge.
Austfonna's ice front runs for well over 100 km, almost without a break.
Austfonna is one of the largest ice caps in Europe.

q.q: What did Bråsvellbreen do in 1936–38?

ne-gl-cambria-icefield.t: An icefield feeding blue glaciers above Stewart
ne-gl-cambria-icefield.s: South-east of the little port of Stewart, at the head of the long fjord of Portland Canal, the Cambria Icefield covers some 700 km² of the Coast Mountains. Its glaciers spill down on all sides into forested valleys. One of them, Bear Glacier, ends right beside a highway, its snout glowing an intense blue above a meltwater lake.
ne-gl-cambria-icefield.w: A white icefield among jagged coastal peaks, glaciers radiating into green valleys, east of a long, narrow fjord.
f: Portland Canal, the fjord below, is more than 100 km long and forms part of the Alaska–Canada border.
Stewart, at the fjord's head, calls itself Canada's northernmost ice-free port.
Its outlet glaciers have been retreating since the early 1900s.

q.q: Which Cambria glacier ends beside a highway near Stewart?

ne-gl-columbia-icefield.t: The rooftop of the Rockies, draining to three oceans
ne-gl-columbia-icefield.s: The Columbia Icefield is the largest in the Rocky Mountains, some 200 km² of ice on the Continental Divide between Alberta and British Columbia. Its meltwater runs to three oceans: west to the Pacific, north to the Arctic, and east through Hudson Bay to the Atlantic. Look for the Athabasca Glacier, a broad white tongue ending near the Icefields Parkway.
ne-gl-columbia-icefield.w: A high white plateau of ice ringed by rock peaks, with a broad glacier tongue reaching down toward a road.
f: Mount Columbia, 3,747 m, on its rim, is the highest point in Alberta.
Snow Dome, on the icefield, is a triple divide: its meltwater can reach three different oceans.
The Athabasca Glacier has retreated more than 1.5 km since the late 1800s.

q.q: How many oceans does Columbia Icefield meltwater reach?

ne-gl-devon-ice-cap.t: Ice on the largest uninhabited island on Earth
ne-gl-devon-ice-cap.s: Devon Island, north of Lancaster Sound, is the largest island on Earth with no permanent residents, and its eastern part lies under the Devon Ice Cap, about 14,000 km² of white. West of the ice the land is a bare, rust-brown plateau, so Mars-like that scientists use the Haughton crater there to rehearse missions to the Red Planet. From the air the white-brown contrast is striking.
ne-gl-devon-ice-cap.w: A white dome covering the eastern end of the island, beside bare, rust-brown plateaus cut by canyons.
f: The Haughton crater, about 23 km wide, was blasted out by an impact tens of millions of years ago.
The Haughton-Mars Project has run field seasons at the crater since 1997.

q.q: What makes Devon Island stand out?

ne-gl-edgeoyjokulen.t: A white dome on Svalbard's wild eastern island
ne-gl-edgeoyjokulen.s: Edgeøya, Svalbard's third-largest island, has no permanent residents, and much of its eastern part lies under ice caps such as Edgeøyjøkulen. Look for a smooth white dome whose edges break into short glaciers reaching the sea, while the west of the island shows bare, terraced brown plateaus. In winter the whole island merges with the frozen sea around it.
ne-gl-edgeoyjokulen.w: A smooth white dome on a big island south-east of Spitsbergen, with short glaciers reaching the sea and bare brown uplands.
f: The island is named after Thomas Edge, an English merchant in the 17th-century whaling trade.
Edgeøya lies within a nature reserve where polar bears roam freely.

q.q: Where does Edgeøya rank among Svalbard's islands by size?

ne-gl-harding-icefield.t: A frozen sea spilling dozens of glaciers
ne-gl-harding-icefield.s: On the Kenai Peninsula south of Anchorage, the Harding Icefield buries some 1,800 km² of mountains, with only rocky summits poking through. More than 30 glaciers flow off it, several all the way down to the fjords of Kenai Fjords National Park. From above it is a white sea studded with dark islands of rock — nunataks — that ends abruptly at the green coast.
ne-gl-harding-icefield.w: A white expanse dotted with dark rock peaks, sending glacier tongues down to fjords on the Kenai Peninsula's south coast.
f: It is named after US President Warren G. Harding, who visited Alaska in 1923.
Exit Glacier, near the town of Seward, is the one part of the icefield you can reach by road.

q.q: Which national park lies below the Harding Icefield?

ne-gl-holtedahlfonna.t: The ice field that feeds the glaciers of Kongsfjorden
ne-gl-holtedahlfonna.s: North-west Spitsbergen is crowned by Holtedahlfonna, the island's second-largest ice cap, about 1,400 km² of white. Its ice drains west through Kronebreen, one of Svalbard's fastest glaciers, which ends in a crumbling blue wall at the head of Kongsfjorden. On the same fjord stands Ny-Ålesund, one of the northernmost research settlements on Earth.
ne-gl-holtedahlfonna.w: A broad white ice field east of Kongsfjorden, sending a wide glacier into the head of the fjord.
f: It is named after the Norwegian geologist Olaf Holtedahl.
Kronebreen can flow up to about 3 m a day.
Ny-Ålesund hosts research stations from about ten countries.

q.q: Which fast glacier drains Holtedahlfonna into Kongsfjorden?

ne-gl-juneau-icefield.t: The icefield behind Alaska's roadless capital
ne-gl-juneau-icefield.s: Right behind Juneau, Alaska's capital, the mountains vanish under the Juneau Icefield, nearly 4,000 km² of ice straddling the US–Canada border. Dozens of glaciers pour off it: the Mendenhall reaches almost to the city's suburbs, and the Taku runs down toward the sea. The ice is one reason no road links Juneau to the rest of North America.
ne-gl-juneau-icefield.w: A white plateau with dark peaks behind Juneau, glaciers spilling toward the sea, one ending in a lake by the town.
f: Juneau is the only US state capital on the North American mainland with no road link to the rest of the continent.
Students have studied the icefield every summer since the late 1940s through the Juneau Icefield Research Program.
For decades the Taku was one of the few advancing glaciers in Alaska.

q.q: Which Juneau Icefield glacier ends in a lake near the city?

ne-gl-karpinsky-ice-cap.t: Severnaya Zemlya's highest point is made of ice
ne-gl-karpinsky-ice-cap.s: The Karpinsky Ice Cap is the largest of the seven ice caps on October Revolution Island, about 2,800 km². Its summit, at about 965 m, is the highest point of the whole Severnaya Zemlya archipelago — and it is ice, not rock. Look for a broad dome sloping toward the Laptev Sea, its edges split into outlet glaciers and bays choked with sea ice most of the year.
ne-gl-karpinsky-ice-cap.w: A broad white dome on the eastern side of a large Arctic island, with glaciers reaching into ice-choked bays.
f: It is named after Alexander Karpinsky, a geologist who became the first elected president of the Russian Academy of Sciences.
October Revolution Island is the largest island of Severnaya Zemlya.

q.q: What forms the highest point of Severnaya Zemlya?

ne-gl-kluane-ice-cap.t: The biggest icefields outside the polar regions
ne-gl-kluane-ice-cap.s: Between Yukon and Alaska lies a sea of ice that swallows whole mountain ranges: the icefields of the Saint Elias Mountains, the largest outside the polar regions. Rising from them is Mount Logan, 5,959 m, Canada's highest peak and one of the bulkiest mountains on Earth. From above look for rivers of ice many kilometres wide, striped with dark moraines like highways.
ne-gl-kluane-ice-cap.w: Endless white icefields with dark rock peaks and huge striped glaciers, inland from the Gulf of Alaska.
f: Kluane National Park and its neighbours form a single UNESCO World Heritage site straddling the Canada–US border.
Mount Logan is thought to have the largest base of any non-volcanic mountain on Earth.
The Hubbard Glacier, fed from these icefields, calves into the sea near Yakutat.

q.q: Which mountain, rising from these icefields, is Canada's highest?

ne-gl-lyell-icefield.t: Five summits named for Swiss mountain guides
ne-gl-lyell-icefield.s: South of the Columbia Icefield, another sheet of ice spreads along the Continental Divide: the Lyell Icefield. Above it rise the five summits of Mount Lyell, named after the geologist Charles Lyell; the individual peaks honour Swiss guides who worked in the Canadian Rockies. Look for a white plateau feeding glaciers west into British Columbia and east into the valleys of Banff National Park.
ne-gl-lyell-icefield.w: A white ice plateau on the Rockies' crest south of the larger Columbia Icefield, with glaciers pouring off both sides.
f: Charles Lyell, whose name it bears, was one of the founders of modern geology.
Its eastern glaciers feed the North Saskatchewan River, whose water ends up in Hudson Bay.

q.q: Which river is fed by the Lyell Icefield's eastern glaciers?

ne-gl-malaspina-glacier.t: A giant fan of ice spread over the Alaskan plain
ne-gl-malaspina-glacier.s: Look for a vast, round lobe of ice sprawled across the coastal plain at the foot of Mount Saint Elias: the Malaspina, the largest piedmont glacier in the world. The Seward Glacier squeezes out of the mountains through a gap and spreads like dough on a table, about 65 km wide. Its surface is marbled with dark bands of moraine, folded into zigzags by repeated surges.
ne-gl-malaspina-glacier.w: A huge rounded lobe of ice on the coastal plain, marbled with dark zigzag stripes, west of Yakutat Bay.
f: It covers about 3,900 km², more than the US state of Rhode Island.
It is named after Alessandro Malaspina, who explored this coast for Spain in 1791.
Its bed lies below sea level, so the ocean could one day flood in if the ice thins enough.

q.q: What kind of glacier is the Malaspina?

ne-gl-manson-icefield.t: A lonely ice sheet on Ellesmere's southern shore
ne-gl-manson-icefield.s: Along the south-east coast of Ellesmere Island, at the top of Baffin Bay, the Manson Icefield covers roughly 6,000 km² of mountains. From above it is a broad white plateau whose glaciers drop steeply into the sea, calving icebergs that drift slowly south. There are no roads or settlements on the ice, and in winter it merges with the frozen sea into a single white plain.
ne-gl-manson-icefield.w: A broad white plateau on Ellesmere's south-east coast, with glaciers dropping steeply into dark, ice-strewn water.
f: Grise Fiord, Canada's northernmost civilian community, lies on the same southern coast of Ellesmere.
Just offshore, the North Water polynya is a stretch of sea that stays partly open even in winter.

q.q: Which is Canada's northernmost civilian community, on Ellesmere?

ne-gl-monarch-icefield.t: A crown of ice above the Bella Coola valley
ne-gl-monarch-icefield.s: South-east of the fjord town of Bella Coola, the Coast Mountains vanish under the Monarch Icefield, the northernmost of a chain of big icefields in the Pacific Ranges. Its namesake, Monarch Mountain, 3,555 m, towers over the peaks around it. From above, look for a white plateau with dark summits, glaciers spilling toward deep green valleys, and the long fjords of the coast beyond.
ne-gl-monarch-icefield.w: A white icefield with dark rock summits south-east of a long fjord, glaciers draining toward deep green valleys.
f: Henry Hall and Hans Fuhrer made the first ascent of Monarch Mountain in 1936.
The larger Ha-Iltzuk Icefield, the biggest of this group, lies to the south.
The Bella Coola valley below is known for grizzly bears fishing for salmon.

q.q: Which fjord town lies north-west of the Monarch Icefield?

ne-gl-mount-brown-icefield.t: Home of a famous mountain-height blunder
ne-gl-mount-brown-icefield.s: Around Athabasca Pass on the Continental Divide lies the Mount Brown Icefield, a quiet sheet of ice in the backcountry south of Jasper. Its namesake has a story: in 1827 the Scottish botanist David Douglas declared Mount Brown and its neighbour Mount Hooker to be about 16,000 feet high, the tallest peaks in North America. For decades maps repeated the claim. Both are in fact well under 3,500 m.
ne-gl-mount-brown-icefield.w: A white icefield among dark peaks on the Rockies' crest, beside a low notch that marks an old fur-trade pass.
f: Athabasca Pass was a main fur-trade route across the Rockies in the early 1800s.
Mount Brown is named after the botanist Robert Brown, known for describing Brownian motion.
The myth of the giant peaks lasted until climbers and surveyors checked them in the 1890s.

q.q: What did David Douglas get wrong about Mount Brown in 1827?

ne-gl-muller-ice-cap.t: Arctic ice on an island of fossil forests
ne-gl-muller-ice-cap.s: Axel Heiberg Island, west of Ellesmere, is crowned by two ice caps, and the Müller is the northern one. Its outlet glaciers creep down toward long fjords. Nearby, White Glacier has been measured every year since 1959, one of the longest such records in the Arctic. Elsewhere on the island lie mummified tree stumps from forests that grew here some 45 million years ago.
ne-gl-muller-ice-cap.w: A broad white ice cap in northern Axel Heiberg Island, glaciers reaching down toward long, dark fjords.
f: The island is named after Axel Heiberg, a Norwegian brewery director who funded Otto Sverdrup's expedition.
McGill University has run a summer research station at Expedition Fiord since 1960.

q.q: What remarkable fossils have been found on Axel Heiberg Island?

ne-gl-myrdalsjokull.t: An ice cap hiding the volcano Katla
ne-gl-myrdalsjokull.s: Near Iceland's southern tip, a round white cap of ice sits above black sand plains: Mýrdalsjökull, about 500 km². Beneath it lies Katla, one of Iceland's most powerful volcanoes, which last erupted in a big way in 1918, sending floods of meltwater across the coast. Just to the west is the smaller Eyjafjallajökull, whose 2010 eruption grounded flights across Europe for days.
ne-gl-myrdalsjokull.w: A rounded white ice cap above black sand plains on Iceland's south coast, with smaller Eyjafjallajökull just to the west.
f: The 1918 Katla flood carried so much sediment that it pushed the shoreline several kilometres out to sea.
Vík, near its southern foot, is the southernmost village in Iceland.
Mýrdalsjökull is Iceland's fourth-largest glacier.

q.q: Which volcano lies beneath Mýrdalsjökull?

ne-gl-negribreen.t: A glacier that wakes up about once a century
ne-gl-negribreen.s: On Spitsbergen's east coast, Negribreen flows into the wide Storfjorden, a broad river of ice with a heavily crevassed surface. It is a surge-type glacier: in 1935–36 it lurched almost 12 km forward in a single year. In 2016 it woke again, and by 2017 parts were racing along at about 20 m a day. From above look for a chaotic, shattered surface of white ice blocks.
ne-gl-negribreen.w: A broad, heavily crevassed glacier on Spitsbergen's east coast, ending in an ice cliff in the wide Storfjorden.
f: In its 1935–36 surge the front advanced along a stretch about 15 km wide.
Surging glaciers are common in Svalbard; many lie quiet for decades between surges.

q.q: How far did Negribreen lurch forward in 1935–36?

ne-gl-north-ellesmere-ice-cap.t: Ice at the very top of North America
ne-gl-north-ellesmere-ice-cap.s: The northern end of Ellesmere Island is some of the northernmost land on Earth, and much of it lies under ice caps and icefields. Here, in Quttinirpaaq National Park, rise the highest mountains of the Canadian Arctic, including Barbeau Peak, 2,616 m. From above look for white plateaus broken by dark nunataks and, along the coast, the ragged remains of ancient floating ice shelves.
ne-gl-north-ellesmere-ice-cap.w: White plateaus pierced by dark peaks, fringed along the Arctic Ocean coast by the remains of floating ice shelves.
f: Cape Columbia, on Ellesmere's north coast, is the northernmost point of Canada.
Quttinirpaaq means 'top of the world' in Inuktitut.
Barbeau Peak, 2,616 m, is the highest mountain in Nunavut.

q.q: What does 'Quttinirpaaq' mean in Inuktitut?

ne-gl-northern-patagonian-ice-field.t: Where a glacier meets the sea closest to the equator
ne-gl-northern-patagonian-ice-field.s: The Northern Patagonian Ice Field is the smaller of Patagonia's two great ice fields, yet it still drapes some 4,000 km² of ice over the Andes of southern Chile. Its highest point, Monte San Valentín, about 4,000 m, is the tallest summit in Patagonia. On its western side the San Rafael Glacier reaches Laguna San Rafael, a lagoon open to the Pacific, at only about 46.7° south.
ne-gl-northern-patagonian-ice-field.w: An icy plateau on the Andes of southern Chile, glaciers spilling west to a milky lagoon and east toward turquoise lakes.
f: San Rafael is often called the tidewater glacier closest to the equator.
Lake General Carrera, east of the ice field, is the largest lake in Chile.

q.q: Which is the highest summit of the Northern Patagonian Ice Field?

ne-gl-penny-ice-cap.t: The ice cap of 'the land that never melts'
ne-gl-penny-ice-cap.s: On Baffin Island's Cumberland Peninsula, the Penny Ice Cap spreads some 6,000 km² of white just north of the Arctic Circle. It is the heart of Auyuittuq National Park — 'the land that never melts' in Inuktitut. From its edges glaciers pour down into deep U-shaped valleys and fjords, walled by some of the tallest granite cliffs on Earth.
ne-gl-penny-ice-cap.w: A broad white ice cap feeding glaciers into deep, steep-walled valleys, just north of the Arctic Circle on Baffin Island.
f: Mount Thor, in the park, has one of the tallest sheer cliffs on Earth, about 1,250 m.
Akshayuk Pass, a well-known trekking route, cuts right across the peninsula below the ice.

q.q: What does Auyuittuq mean in Inuktitut?

ne-gl-prince-of-wales-icefield.t: A vast ice sheet on Ellesmere, facing Greenland
ne-gl-prince-of-wales-icefield.s: The Prince of Wales Icefield spreads along the eastern side of central Ellesmere Island, roughly 20,000 km² of ice — larger than many small countries. Across the channels to the east lies Greenland. From above, look for an immense white plateau split by outlet glaciers that snake down to the sea, releasing icebergs into the ice-choked straits.
ne-gl-prince-of-wales-icefield.w: An immense white plateau on eastern Ellesmere, with glaciers snaking east to the sea channels that separate it from Greenland.
f: It is one of the largest icefields in the Canadian Arctic.
Smith Sound and Nares Strait, off its eastern side, link Baffin Bay with the Arctic Ocean.

q.q: Which land lies across the strait east of this icefield?

ne-gl-sargent-icefield.t: Glaciers pouring straight into Prince William Sound
ne-gl-sargent-icefield.s: On the eastern Kenai Peninsula, the Sargent Icefield caps the mountains above the maze of fjords and islands of Prince William Sound. Its glaciers spill down steep valleys right to the sea, calving icebergs into quiet green inlets. Some carry unexpected names: Princeton Glacier, for example, was named in 1909 after the university.
ne-gl-sargent-icefield.w: A white icefield above a maze of fjords and forested islands, with glaciers ending at the water's edge.
f: It is named after Rufus Harvey Sargent, a US Geological Survey mapmaker who surveyed the Kenai Peninsula.
Chenega Glacier, one of its outlets, takes its name from nearby Chenega Island.

q.q: Which sound do the Sargent Icefield's glaciers flow into?

ne-gl-southern-patagonian-ice-field.t: The largest ice in the south outside Antarctica
ne-gl-southern-patagonian-ice-field.s: For some 350 km along the Andes, the mountains of Patagonia disappear under one continuous sheet of ice, the largest in the Southern Hemisphere outside Antarctica. On a clear day you can follow glaciers flowing west to Pacific fjords and east to milky turquoise lakes in Argentina. Granite spires such as Fitz Roy and the Torres del Paine rise from its edges like broken teeth.
ne-gl-southern-patagonian-ice-field.w: A continuous white sheet on the Andes, glaciers streaming west to fjords and east into turquoise lakes like Lago Argentino.
f: Perito Moreno Glacier, one of its outlets, ends in an ice wall about 5 km wide in Lago Argentino.
Pío XI, on the Chilean side, is the largest glacier in South America.

q.q: Which famous glacier of this ice field ends in Lago Argentino?

ne-gl-steacie-ice-cap.t: The southern ice cap of an uninhabited Arctic island
ne-gl-steacie-ice-cap.s: Axel Heiberg Island, west of Ellesmere, carries two big ice caps, and the Steacie covers the island's southern highlands. From above it is a broad white dome, its outlet glaciers winding between dark, flat-topped plateaus toward the fjords. Nobody lives on the island; in summer only a few research camps dot its valleys, and in winter the sea around it freezes solid.
ne-gl-steacie-ice-cap.w: A broad white dome over southern Axel Heiberg Island, glaciers winding between dark flat-topped plateaus to the fjords.
f: More than a quarter of Axel Heiberg Island, some 43,000 km² in all, lies under ice.
Several glaciers on the island's west side have kept advancing for decades, against the global trend.

q.q: Axel Heiberg Island lies next to which larger island?

ne-gl-stikine-icecap.t: An icefield split by a wild river
ne-gl-stikine-icecap.s: Along the Alaska–British Columbia border near Wrangell and Petersburg, the Stikine Icecap buries the Coast Mountains in white. The Stikine River slices right through the range here, one of only a few rivers that do. On the Alaskan side LeConte Glacier reaches the sea, calving icebergs into LeConte Bay. Look too for Devils Thumb, a sharp rock spire rising from the ice on the border.
ne-gl-stikine-icecap.w: A broad white icefield on the coastal mountains east of Petersburg, cut by a wide river valley and fjords full of icebergs.
f: LeConte Glacier is the southernmost tidewater glacier in the Northern Hemisphere.
John Muir compared the Stikine valley to 'a Yosemite a hundred miles long'.

q.q: Which glacier here is the Northern Hemisphere's southernmost tidewater glacier?

ne-gl-university-ice-cap.t: One of seven ice caps on a remote Arctic island
ne-gl-university-ice-cap.s: October Revolution Island, the largest of Severnaya Zemlya, wears seven ice caps, and the University Ice Cap lies south of the biggest, the Karpinsky. Its dome rises to about 800 m. Between the caps the bare ground is stony polar desert, brown and grey in summer, with no trees or shrubs at all. In winter everything merges with the frozen seas into one white expanse.
ne-gl-university-ice-cap.w: A white dome on a large Arctic island, flanked by stony brown polar desert and other ice caps to the north.
f: Severnaya Zemlya separates the Kara Sea from the Laptev Sea.
The archipelago was mapped only in 1930–32, by a four-man expedition led by Georgy Ushakov.

q.q: Which two seas does Severnaya Zemlya separate?

ne-gl-vatnajokull.t: Iceland's giant ice cap, sitting on volcanoes
ne-gl-vatnajokull.s: Vatnajökull covers about 8% of Iceland, some 7,700 km² of ice up to nearly a kilometre thick. From above it is a white plateau spilling glacier tongues in every direction, some ending in lagoons full of icebergs near the south coast. Beneath the ice lie active volcanoes, including Grímsvötn and Bárðarbunga, whose eruptions can melt the ice and unleash sudden floods.
ne-gl-vatnajokull.w: A vast white ice cap in south-east Iceland, glacier tongues radiating outward and a lagoon of icebergs by the coast.
f: Hvannadalshnúkur, on its southern rim, is Iceland's highest peak at about 2,110 m.
Jökulsárlón, the lagoon at the foot of one of its glaciers, is crowded with floating icebergs.
Vatnajökull National Park became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2019.

q.q: Which Icelandic volcano lies beneath Vatnajökull?

ne-gl-vestfonna.t: The western twin of Svalbard's great ice caps
ne-gl-vestfonna.s: Nordaustlandet, Svalbard's second-largest island, is mostly wrapped in ice, split between two great caps. Vestfonna, the western one, covers about 2,500 km²: a low white dome crossed by ridges and outlet glaciers that end in ice cliffs along the fjords. Its bigger sibling, Austfonna, spreads to the east, and together they make the island look frosted from above.
ne-gl-vestfonna.w: A low white dome on the western half of a large, ice-covered island north-east of Spitsbergen.
f: Nordaustlandet has no permanent residents and is protected as a nature reserve.
Walruses haul out on beaches along the island's coasts.

q.q: Which is Vestfonna's larger neighbour on the same island?

Q358755.t: A huge snowy volcano named after a rare bird
Q358755.s: Mount Takahe is a broad shield volcano rising alone from the ice of Marie Byrd Land, 3,460 m high and with a volume of about 780 km³. From above it looks like a gently swelling white dome with a wide, shallow crater on top. Its last known eruption was about 7,500 years ago, and layers of its ash turn up in Antarctic ice cores.
Q358755.w: A broad, gently rounded snow dome rising alone from the flat ice, with a wide shallow crater at its summit.
f: It is named after the takahē, a rare flightless bird of New Zealand.
Its summit caldera is about 8 km across.

q.q: What is Mount Takahe named after?

Q924312.t: Antarctica's highest volcano, with a broken crater
Q924312.s: Mount Sidley is the tallest of the Executive Committee Range, a line of volcanoes standing in the ice of Marie Byrd Land, and at 4,285 m it is the highest volcano in Antarctica. Its south side is torn open by a caldera about 5 km wide, a dramatic bite out of the white cone. Richard Byrd spotted it from the air in 1934.
Q924312.w: A massive white volcano in a north–south line of snowy cones, its southern flank cut by a huge crater.
f: Byrd named it after Mabelle Sidley, daughter of one of his expedition's sponsors.
It is the Antarctic entry on the 'Volcanic Seven Summits', the highest volcano on each continent.
The first recorded ascent was made in 1990.

q.q: Which is the highest volcano in Antarctica?

Q3321842.t: A giant beside Amundsen's road to the Pole
Q3321842.s: In November 1911 Roald Amundsen's party climbed from the Ross Ice Shelf up the Axel Heiberg Glacier toward the polar plateau, and beside their route stood this massive peak. Amundsen named it after Fridtjof Nansen, the Norwegian explorer who had lent him his ship, the Fram. At 4,069 m it is one of the great summits of the Queen Maud Mountains, a wall of rock and ice across the way to the Pole.
Q3321842.w: A massive ice-clad peak at the edge of the Ross Ice Shelf, beside a steep glacier climbing toward the polar plateau.
f: Amundsen reached the South Pole on 14 December 1911, about a month after passing this mountain.
The Axel Heiberg Glacier beside it climbs roughly 3,000 m from the ice shelf to the plateau.

q.q: Who named Mount Fridtjof Nansen in 1911?

Q19459387.t: The high point above Pangong's blue lake
Q19459387.s: Kangju Kangri is the highest summit of the Pangong Range, 6,725 m, a white crest in the high desert of eastern Ladakh. Its most striking neighbour is water rather than rock: Pangong Tso, a narrow lake some 130 km long at about 4,200 m, lies at its foot. From above the lake is an unmistakable ribbon of blue that shifts from turquoise to deep navy with the light.
Q19459387.w: A white crest in bare brown mountains beside a long, narrow, vividly blue lake that winds away to the east.
f: Pangong Tso is brackish, yet it freezes over in winter.
Kangju Kangri was first climbed in 1983.
Villagers on the lake's southern shore also call the peak Thinguru.

q.q: Which long high-altitude lake lies at the foot of Kangju Kangri?

Q28794266.t: The 'white mountain' of the central Kunlun
Q28794266.s: Aktag means 'white mountain' in Turkic, a plain name for a remote summit in the Kunlun, the long range that walls the Tibetan Plateau off from the Tarim Basin. At 6,748 m it is among the highest peaks of the Kunlun, rising in one of the least visited corners of Asia. From above look for a white massif over khaki ridges, with the sandy Tarim lowlands far to the north.
Q28794266.w: A white massif rising from bare khaki ridges, with the pale desert lowlands of the Tarim Basin far to the north.
f: The Kunlun runs for more than 2,000 km along the northern rim of the Tibetan Plateau.
North of the range lies the Taklamakan, one of the largest sand deserts in the world.
