q.q: What does the Turkic name Aktag mean?

ne-pk-1159105667.t: The sacred giant the Yellow River bends around
ne-pk-1159105667.s: Amne Machin is the holy mountain of the Golog Tibetans, a broad massif of ice rising to 6,282 m from the grasslands of Qinghai. The Yellow River, flowing east from its source, swings in a great loop around the range before turning north. Pilgrims walk a long circuit around it. From above look for a white crest of glaciers ringed by high green pastures.
ne-pk-1159105667.w: A broad ice massif in rolling green-brown grassland, with a big river looping around it in a wide bend.
f: Early 20th-century explorers guessed it might rival Everest; modern surveys put it at 6,282 m.
Amne means 'grandfather' in the local Amdo dialect, an honorific for the mountain's protector deity.

q.q: Which great river loops around the Amne Machin range?

Q724367.t: Siberia's highest peak, twin-topped and white
Q724367.s: Belukha is the highest mountain of the Altai and of all Siberia, 4,506 m, straddling the border of Russia and Kazakhstan. Its name comes from its whiteness: two snowy summits joined by a saddle, draped in glaciers that feed the Katun, one of the rivers that form the Ob. From above, look for a bright white crown standing over greener, lower ridges and turquoise lakes.
Q724367.w: A twin-summited white massif above green valleys and turquoise lakes, on the Russia–Kazakhstan border in the Altai.
f: The Katun River begins at the Gebler Glacier on Belukha's southern side.
The Tronov brothers made the first ascent of the eastern summit in 1914.
Belukha is part of the Golden Mountains of Altai, a UNESCO World Heritage site.

q.q: Which river rises from the glaciers of Belukha?

Q4062402.t: A lonely ice massif in Tibet's far west
Q4062402.s: Far out in the dry uplands of western Tibet, the Nganglong massif rises to about 6,720 m, a knot of ice with more than 40 peaks over 6,000 m. It stands roughly 85 km east-north-east of the town of Ali, in a land of gravel plains and salt lakes. From above, look for a cluster of white summits and glaciers set in a vast brown landscape.
Q4062402.w: A cluster of white summits and glaciers in a vast brown upland of gravel plains, north-east of the town of Ali.
f: The massif holds 37 glaciers, two of them more than 6 km long.
Modern Chinese maps give about 6,720 m, although older sources still quote 7,315 m.

q.q: Which town lies about 85 km west-south-west of the Nganglong massif?

Q5530346.t: Where the Yangtze is born, in Tibet's ice
Q5530346.s: The longest river in Asia starts here. Meltwater from glaciers on Geladaindong, the highest peak of the Tanggula Mountains at 6,621 m, gathers into the Tuotuo River, the traditional source of the Yangtze. From this cold, empty upland the water will travel more than 6,000 km to the sea at Shanghai. Look for a white massif of glaciers above braided silver streams on the brown plateau.
Q5530346.w: A white massif of glaciers above braided silver streams spreading across the brown plateau of central Tibet.
f: The Jianggendiru Glacier on its south-west flank is usually named as the Yangtze's source.
East of the peak, the Qinghai–Tibet railway crosses the Tanggula range at about 5,070 m.

q.q: Which great river begins on Geladaindong's glaciers?

Q2102394.t: A remote ice peak of the eastern Karakoram
Q2102394.s: This summit of the eastern Karakoram, charted at 6,934 m and known as Shahi Kangri, stands above the upper Shyok valley in Ladakh, west of the high, empty plains of Aksai Chin. It is a world of ice and bare rock: glaciers pour down between brown ridges, and the braided Shyok threads its gravel bed below. The higher Saser Kangri group rises to the south.
Q2102394.w: Glaciers and white crests above a braided grey river valley, with bare brown plateaus stretching away to the east.
f: Saser Kangri I, the highest summit of the neighbouring Saser group, reaches about 7,670 m.
The Shyok River, flowing below, is a major tributary of the Indus.

q.q: The Shyok River below this peak is a tributary of which river?

Q2118899.t: The biggest ice field of Tibet's empty north
Q2118899.s: In the heart of the Changtang, the high, cold and almost empty north of Tibet, Purog Kangri rises to 6,929 m above a dome of ice some 400 km² in area. It is the largest ice field of the northern Tibetan Plateau. From above it looks like a white starfish on a brown plain, its glacier arms reaching out toward shallow lakes and salt flats.
Q2118899.w: A white, star-shaped ice field with radiating glacier lobes on the brown plateau, surrounded by lakes and salt flats.
f: In 2000 Chinese and American scientists drilled ice cores here, the longest 213 m deep.
The ice field holds about 52 km³ of ice.

q.q: In which remote region of Tibet does Purog Kangri lie?

Q4848635.t: The unclimbed crown of a hidden Tibetan range
Q4848635.s: In the wet, deeply cut south-east of Tibet rises the Kangri Garpo range, and Bairiga, 6,882 m, is its highest peak. It has never been climbed. The range was so little known that until 2009 none of its 47 summits above 6,000 m had been reached. From above look for a chain of white peaks feeding long glaciers, their tongues reaching down toward dark forested valleys.
Q4848635.w: A chain of white peaks with long glaciers reaching down toward dark, forested valleys in south-eastern Tibet.
f: The botanist-explorer Frank Kingdon-Ward photographed the peak in 1933, when it was known as Choembo.
The Lhagu Glacier, the largest in the range, is about 30 km long.

q.q: Bairiga is the highest peak of which range?

Q572801.t: A modest mountain with famously savage weather
Q572801.s: At 1,917 m Mount Washington is small by world standards, yet it is the highest peak in the north-eastern United States and notorious for its weather. Storm tracks from several directions converge over the Presidential Range, and in April 1934 observers on the summit measured a gust of 372 km/h. From above look for a bare grey summit ridge above New Hampshire's dark green forests, often white from October to May.
Q572801.w: A bare grey summit ridge above endless dark forest in northern New Hampshire, the tallest of a chain of treeless peaks.
f: The 1934 gust of 231 mph stood as the world's strongest measured wind for over 60 years.
The Mount Washington Cog Railway, opened in 1869, was the world's first mountain-climbing cog railway.
The harsh climate keeps the treeline here at only about 1,300 m.

q.q: What record did Mount Washington's summit set in 1934?

Q1858056.t: The finish line of the Appalachian Trail
Q1858056.s: Katahdin rises alone from the forests and lakes of northern Maine, a granite massif of 1,606 m with a bare, bouldery top. Its name means 'the greatest mountain' in the Penobscot language. For hikers it is the northern end of the Appalachian Trail, which runs about 3,500 km from Georgia. From above, look for its grey summit plateau and sharp ridges above dark green woods.
Q1858056.w: A lone grey granite massif rising from dark forest dotted with countless lakes in northern Maine.
f: Henry David Thoreau climbed toward its summit in 1846 and wrote about it in The Maine Woods.
Former governor Percival Baxter bought the land around it and gave it to Maine as a park.
The trail's southern end is Springer Mountain in Georgia.

q.q: Which long-distance trail ends on Katahdin?

Q748355.t: A lone volcano ruling northern California
Q748355.s: Mount Shasta stands alone, a huge white cone rising some 3,000 m above the surrounding country of northern California. At 4,322 m it is the second-highest peak of the Cascades and the largest of their stratovolcanoes by volume. Look for a smaller cone, Shastina, bulging from its western flank; on a clear day the pair can be seen from well over 100 km away.
Q748355.w: A lone white volcanic cone with a smaller cone on its western shoulder, rising far above forested plateaus.
f: Shastina, its satellite cone, would rank among the Cascades' tallest volcanoes on its own.
Its Whitney Glacier is the longest glacier in California.

q.q: What is the name of Shasta's satellite cone?

Q2078034.t: A wall of peaks with no foothills at all
Q2078034.s: The Tetons rise straight out of the flat valley of Jackson Hole with no foothills in between, and Grand Teton, 4,199 m, is the sharpest tooth among them. The range stands about 2,100 m above the valley floor, pushed up along a fault that is still active. From above look for a jagged grey line of peaks, with the blue ovals of Jackson Lake and smaller glacial lakes along its eastern foot.
Q2078034.w: A short, jagged range rising abruptly from a flat valley, with lakes along its eastern foot, just south of Yellowstone.
f: French-speaking fur trappers called the peaks les trois tétons, 'the three breasts'.
The Teton Range is among the youngest in the Rocky Mountains, less than 10 million years old.
Yellowstone National Park lies just to the north.

q.q: Which valley lies at the eastern foot of the Tetons?

Q275662.t: Portland's snowy volcano, skiable even in summer
Q275662.s: Mount Hood is Oregon's highest peak, about 3,400 m, a sharp snowy volcano some 80 km east of Portland that crowns the city's skyline on clear days. It is still considered potentially active, with steam vents near the summit. On its south slope the Palmer Snowfield keeps skiers busy well into summer, and Timberline Lodge, built in the 1930s, sits just below the treeline.
Q275662.w: A sharp, lone white cone rising above dark forest, east of Portland and south of the Columbia River Gorge.
f: A British naval officer named it in 1792 after Admiral Samuel Hood.
Its last significant eruptions came in the 1780s, shortly before Europeans arrived.
Timberline Lodge played the exterior of the hotel in the film The Shining.

q.q: Which city sees Mount Hood on its skyline, about 80 km away?

Q756244.t: A snowy giant east of Santiago
Q756244.s: Tupungato is a massive, snow-capped volcano over 6,500 m high, straddling the border of Chile and Argentina east of Santiago. It is an old, eroded giant; its smaller, younger neighbour, Tupungatito, has erupted repeatedly in the last two centuries. From above look for a broad white massif rising from a tangle of dry brown Andean ridges, with green vineyards in the valleys on the Argentine side.
Q756244.w: A broad white massif on the Chile–Argentina border, rising above dry brown ridges about 80 km east of Santiago.
f: Matthias Zurbriggen and Stuart Vines made the first ascent in 1897.
The Argentine wine district of Tupungato, in the Uco Valley, takes its name from the volcano.

q.q: Who made the first ascent of Tupungato in 1897?

Q233836.t: The highest volcano on Earth, in the driest desert
Q233836.s: Ojos del Salado is the highest volcano on Earth, nearly 6,900 m, rising on the border of Chile and Argentina at the edge of the Atacama. The air here is so dry that the mountain carries only thin patches of snow despite its height. Steaming vents near the summit show it is not extinct. From above look for a broad, pale massif in a moonscape of ochre, rust and white salt flats.
Q233836.w: A broad, pale volcanic massif in a moonscape of ochre and rust, with white salt flats spread around it.
f: It is also the highest point of Chile.
A small crater lake near the summit, at about 6,390 m, is often called the highest lake in the world.

q.q: Which country's highest point is Ojos del Salado?

Q214916.t: An Inca shrine on a volcano in the sky
Q214916.s: Llullaillaco rises to 6,739 m on the border of Chile and Argentina, in one of the driest places on Earth. Five centuries ago the Inca climbed to its summit to build a shrine, and in 1999 archaeologists found three remarkably preserved Inca burials there — the highest archaeological site in the world. From above look for a lone cone with thin snow above rust-red desert and salt flats.
Q214916.w: A lone, sharp volcanic cone with thin snow patches above rust-red desert and bright salt flats in the Atacama.
f: The three Inca children found on the summit are now kept in a museum in Salta, Argentina.
The air is so dry that snow on the summit often turns straight to vapour without melting.

q.q: What did archaeologists find on Llullaillaco's summit in 1999?

Q148521.t: The snowy guardian on La Paz's skyline
Q148521.s: Illimani is the mountain that seems to appear in every photo of La Paz: a long white wall with several summits, towering over the city and the high plain of El Alto. At about 6,400 m it is the highest peak of the Cordillera Real and the second-highest in Bolivia. From above look for a massive glacier-clad ridge rising south-east of the city, with the dark gash of La Paz's canyon below.
Q148521.w: A long, glacier-clad ridge with several summits, south-east of La Paz and the flat, built-up plateau of El Alto.
f: Martin Conway and two Alpine guides climbed its south summit in 1898.
La Paz and El Alto together form one of the highest large urban areas on Earth, between about 3,600 and 4,100 m.

q.q: Which city lies at the foot of Illimani?

Q272593.t: Bolivia's highest summit, a lone volcanic cone
Q272593.s: Nevado Sajama rises alone from the Altiplano, a white-topped cone of 6,542 m and the highest point of Bolivia. Just to the west, on the Chilean border, two more volcanoes stand side by side, Parinacota and Pomerape, known together as the Payachatas. On Sajama's lower slopes grows one of the highest forests on Earth, made of small, twisted queñua trees.
Q272593.w: A lone, snow-capped volcanic cone on the brown Altiplano, with twin white cones on the Chilean border to its west.
f: Sajama National Park, created in 1939, was Bolivia's first national park.
Ice cores drilled on its summit in 1997 reach back roughly 25,000 years.

q.q: What name is given to the twin volcanoes west of Sajama?

Q758574.t: A volcano once mined almost to its summit
Q758574.s: Aucanquilcha is a big, pale volcano of 6,176 m in the Atacama highlands of northern Chile, and for decades it was a workplace. Sulphur was dug near its summit, at about 5,950 m — for years the highest mine in the world. In 1972 a switchback road for 20-tonne trucks was built almost to the top. From above look for pale yellow-grey slopes above bright white salt flats.
Q758574.w: A broad pale volcano in the dry highlands near the Bolivian border, with white salt flats spread at its foot.
f: The mine opened in 1913, and at first llamas carried the sulphur down the mountain.
The sulphur was refined far below at the camp of Amincha, about 3,900 m, linked by an aerial cableway.

q.q: What was mined near the summit of Aucanquilcha?

Q777794.t: The sacred ice peak beside Rainbow Mountain
Q777794.s: Ausangate is the great white summit of southern Peru, 6,372 m, rising about 100 km south-east of Cusco. For the Quechua people it is an apu, a mountain spirit, and every year thousands of pilgrims gather in a valley near it for the festival of Qoyllur Rit'i. Close by stands Vinicunca, the 'Rainbow Mountain', striped in red, ochre and green.
Q777794.w: A massive white peak rising above brown puna grassland and small turquoise lakes, south-east of Cusco.
f: Ausangate is the highest peak of the Cordillera Vilcanota.
Qoyllur Rit'i, held each year before Corpus Christi, blends Andean and Catholic traditions.
Vinicunca's colours come from layers of mineral-rich sediment.

q.q: Which famous striped mountain lies near Ausangate?

Q946035.t: The largest ice cap in the tropics
Q946035.s: Coropuna is a broad volcanic massif in southern Peru, more than 6,300 m high, crowned by several summits and a sheet of ice. That ice, around 44 km², is the most extensive in the tropics, and its meltwater feeds valleys and farms far below. From above look for a big white cap sprawled over a dark volcanic plateau, north-west of Arequipa.
Q946035.w: A sprawling white ice cap with several summits on a dark volcanic plateau, north-west of Arequipa.
f: Coropuna is the highest volcano in Peru.
The Inca held it sacred, and ruins of their shrines lie on its slopes.
Scientists expect its ice to keep supplying water for roughly another century.

q.q: What record does Coropuna's ice cap hold?
q.a: Largest ice cap in the tropics

Q200935.t: The highest summit in the tropics
Q200935.s: Huascarán is the highest mountain in Peru and in all of the Earth's tropics, 6,768 m. It crowns the Cordillera Blanca, the 'white range', the most heavily glaciated range in the tropics. From above look for a twin-topped white massif towering over the green valley of the Santa River, with turquoise glacial lakes tucked into the side valleys.
Q200935.w: A twin-summited white massif above a long green valley, in a chain of ice peaks running north–south in central Peru.
f: Annie Peck reached its north summit in 1908, a landmark climb for women in mountaineering.
Huascarán National Park became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1985.
The Cordillera Blanca holds hundreds of glacial lakes.

q.q: Which range does Huascarán crown?

Q14081.t: The summit farthest from the centre of the Earth
Q14081.s: Measured from sea level, Chimborazo's 6,267 m is nowhere near Everest. But the Earth bulges at the equator, and this Ecuadorian volcano stands just south of it, so its summit is the point on the planet's surface farthest from the Earth's centre — about 2 km farther out than Everest's. From above look for a broad, glacier-capped dome rising alone over the highlands.
Q14081.w: A broad, glacier-capped volcanic dome standing alone above green and brown highlands, south-west of Quito.
f: In 1802 Alexander von Humboldt climbed to nearly 5,900 m on its slopes, then a world altitude record.
Edward Whymper and his guides Jean-Antoine and Louis Carrel made the first ascent in 1880.

q.q: What makes Chimborazo's summit special?

Q27489229.t: A pale limestone tableland above the Mediterranean
Q27489229.s: Between the Mediterranean and Egypt's Western Desert, the Libyan Plateau spreads as a pale, stony limestone tableland cut by dry wadis. Along the coast it ends in a steep escarpment above a thin strip of shore. From above look for bleached sand-and-stone colours broken only by winding ravines, with the deep blue sea to the north and emptiness to the south.
Q27489229.w: A pale, flat stony plateau cut by dry ravines, ending in a steep escarpment above the blue Mediterranean.
f: To the south-east lies the Qattara Depression, whose floor sinks to about 133 m below sea level.
The plateau's limestone formed on the floor of a sea millions of years ago.
Siwa Oasis, famous in antiquity for its oracle of Amun, lies at the plateau's southern edge.

q.q: Which deep depression lies south-east of the Libyan Plateau?

Q1881042.t: India's mineral heartland of forests and waterfalls
Q1881042.s: East-central India rises into the Chota Nagpur Plateau, a hilly tableland of ancient rock patched with sal forest. It holds much of India's coal and iron ore, so from the air you may spot black scars of open-cast mines and the haze of steel towns. In the monsoon its rivers tumble off the plateau edges in waterfalls, and reservoirs fill the valleys.
Q1881042.w: Rolling green-brown hills and forest patches, with dark open-cast mines, reservoirs and a few hazy industrial towns.
f: Jamshedpur, one of India's first planned industrial cities, grew around a steel works founded here in 1907.
The Damodar valley on the plateau has long been one of India's main coalfields.
Its sal forests are home to many of India's Adivasi communities.

q.q: Which steel city grew up on the Chota Nagpur Plateau from 1907?

Q2740752.t: The highland that keeps the rain off the sertão
Q2740752.s: In north-eastern Brazil, just inland from the green Atlantic coast, the land steps up onto the Borborema Plateau, rolling uplands several hundred metres high. Moist ocean winds drop their rain on its seaward side, so beyond it lies the dry sertão, a land of thorny caatinga scrub. From above you can often see the change: greener to the east, dusty grey-brown to the west.
Q2740752.w: Rolling uplands inland from the coast: greener on the eastern side, grey-brown dry scrub to the west.
f: Campina Grande, on the plateau, hosts one of Brazil's biggest São João festivals every June.
Caatinga, the dry thorny forest beyond, is found only in Brazil.

q.q: Which dry scrubland lies west of the Borborema Plateau?

Q916997.s: The Karoo covers a huge part of South Africa's interior: a semi-desert of flat plains and flat-topped hills capped with dark dolerite. Its name is usually traced to a Khoekhoe word for a dry, thirsty land. From above it is a palette of khaki, rust and grey, crossed by long straight roads and the occasional green thread of a river.
Q916997.w: Flat khaki plains dotted with flat-topped dark hills, crossed by long straight roads and dry riverbeds.
f: Its rocks are rich in fossils of mammal-like reptiles more than 250 million years old.
The MeerKAT radio telescope, part of the Square Kilometre Array project, stands in the Karoo.

q.q: Which giant radio-telescope project is being built in the Karoo?

Q482274.t: Cameroon's water tower, draining three ways
Q482274.s: Across central Cameroon runs the Adamawa Plateau, a high grassy upland mostly around 1,000 m, dotted with old volcanic cones and crater lakes. It is often called Cameroon's water tower: rivers born here flow north toward Lake Chad, west to the Niger by way of the Benue, and south toward the Atlantic and the Congo basin. From above look for green savanna, wooded valleys and red earth.
Q482274.w: A green, rolling upland of savanna and wooded valleys, dotted with small volcanic cones and crater lakes.
f: It is named after Modibo Adama, a Fulani leader who founded an emirate here in the early 19th century.
Ngaoundéré, the main town on the plateau, is the northern end of the railway from Douala.

q.q: Why is the Adamawa Plateau called Cameroon's 'water tower'?

Q776345.t: Angola's high plateau, where the Okavango is born
Q776345.s: The Bié Plateau is the high heart of Angola, rolling grassland and woodland mostly 1,500–1,800 m above the sea. Its rains feed rivers that set off in every direction: the Kwanza to the Atlantic, the Cunene south toward Namibia, and the Cubango, which becomes the Okavango and ends in the sands of Botswana. From above look for green-and-ochre uplands threaded with meandering rivers.
Q776345.w: Rolling green-and-ochre uplands and woodland, laced with meandering rivers and wetlands in central Angola.
f: The Okavango never reaches the sea; it spreads into a vast inland delta in Botswana.
Huambo, on the plateau at about 1,700 m, is one of Angola's largest cities.

q.q: Which famous river starts on the Bié Plateau as the Cubango?

Q1321468.t: An old worn plateau riddled with caves and springs
Q1321468.s: The Ozarks are not really mountains but an old plateau, deeply cut by rivers into forested hills. The limestone beneath is riddled with caves and springs, some of the largest in North America. From above look for dark green, crinkled hill country with winding clear rivers and big, branching reservoirs — dammed valleys shaped like spilled ink.
Q1321468.w: Crinkled, dark green forested hills cut by winding rivers, with large reservoirs spreading in branching, fingered shapes.
f: Missouri, much of it in the Ozarks, has more than 7,000 known caves.
Big Spring in Missouri releases around a billion litres of water on an average day.
The Buffalo River in Arkansas became the first national river in the United States, in 1972.

q.q: Which Ozark river became the first US 'national river' in 1972?

Q4492616.t: A rolling lava plateau of lakes and pine forest
Q4492616.s: Between the Coast Mountains and the Rockies, central British Columbia flattens into the Fraser Plateau, a rolling upland of pine forest, meadows and countless lakes, much of it resting on old lava flows. Along its eastern edge the Fraser River cuts a deep trench on its way to the Pacific. From above look for a green-grey carpet speckled with lakes and slashed by that sharp river canyon.
Q4492616.w: A rolling green-grey upland speckled with lakes, cut on its eastern side by the deep trench of the Fraser River.
f: The Fraser, about 1,375 km long, is the longest river entirely within British Columbia.
In the 2000s a mountain pine beetle outbreak killed vast areas of pine here, turning forests red and then grey.

q.q: Which ocean does the Fraser River finally reach?

Q15241934.t: The continent's ancient shield rock, full of lakes
Q15241934.s: The Laurentian Upland is the worn-down core of the Canadian Shield, a vast sweep of ancient rock around Hudson Bay and the Great Lakes. Ice-age glaciers scraped it bare and left behind a maze of lakes, bogs and rocky knolls. From above, especially near Lake Superior, look for dark forest scattered with thousands of lakes shining like broken glass.
Q15241934.w: Dark forest and bare rock scattered with countless lakes, especially around the shores of Lake Superior.
f: Much of its rock is more than 2.5 billion years old, among the oldest in North America.
Minnesota's Mesabi Range, on the upland, has long been one of the world's great iron-ore districts.
Lake Superior, on its southern edge, is the largest freshwater lake in the world by area.

q.q: Which is the largest freshwater lake by area, on the upland's edge?

Q293730.t: A land of wind-blown yellow dust, carved into gullies
Q293730.s: The Loess Plateau is built of dust: fine yellow silt blown in from the deserts of Central Asia over hundreds of thousands of years, piled in places more than 100 m thick. Rain carves it easily, so from above it looks like a crumpled yellow-brown sheet shot through with branching gullies and neat terraced fields. The silt washing off it gives the Yellow River its colour and its name.
Q293730.w: Crumpled yellow-brown land cut by countless branching gullies, with contour-terraced hillsides and a muddy river.
f: The plateau covers about 640,000 km², larger than Spain.
Millions of people have lived in yaodong, homes dug into the loess hillsides.
A restoration project from the 1990s terraced slopes and replanted hillsides, sharply cutting erosion.

q.q: What gives the Yellow River its colour?

Q1126906.t: Gentle hills of black earth, where great rivers begin
Q1126906.s: South of Moscow the land swells gently into the Central Russian Upland, hills only a couple of hundred metres high but important on the map: the Oka, the Don and tributaries of the Dnieper all start here. Its soils include rich black chernozem. From above look for a patchwork of huge fields cut by branching, tree-lined ravines and, in the south, vast open-pit iron mines.
Q1126906.w: A vast patchwork of fields cut by tree-lined, branching ravines, with huge grey open-pit mines in the south.
f: The Kursk Magnetic Anomaly beneath it is one of the largest iron-ore deposits on Earth.
The Don rises near Novomoskovsk, south of Moscow, and flows about 1,900 km to the Sea of Azov.
Its ravines grow fast because the soft soils erode easily once the forest is cleared.

q.q: Which river rises here and flows to the Sea of Azov?

Q277576.t: A basalt plateau sliced by canyon lakes
Q277576.s: North of the Arctic Circle in Siberia, the Putorana Plateau rises as a giant layer cake of dark basalt, cut into flat-topped mesas by canyons hundreds of metres deep. Many canyons hold long, narrow lakes, like fjords far from any sea. No roads lead in. From above look for stepped cliffs and ribbons of water; in winter the whole plateau becomes black-and-white graphic art.
Q277576.w: Flat-topped dark mesas with stepped sides, cut by deep canyons holding long, narrow lakes, east of Norilsk.
f: The plateau became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2010.
It has the greatest concentration of waterfalls in Russia.
The geographic centre of Russia, at Lake Vivi, lies on its southern edge.

q.q: What lies at Lake Vivi, on the plateau's southern edge?

Q604329.t: Karst hills, rice terraces and eternal spring
Q604329.s: South-west China lifts into the Yunnan–Guizhou Plateau, a high, rumpled land mostly 1,000–2,000 m up, eaten by rain into karst: sinkholes, stone pinnacles and rivers that vanish underground. From above look for green hills pocked with hollows, red-earth fields, big blue lakes around Kunming and, on steep southern slopes, rice terraces stacked like contour lines.
Q604329.w: Rumpled green hills pocked with sinkholes, patches of red earth, and big lakes around the city of Kunming.
f: Kunming, at about 1,900 m, is nicknamed the 'City of Eternal Spring' for its mild climate.
The Stone Forest near Kunming is a maze of grey limestone pillars tens of metres tall.
The Hani rice terraces of Honghe, in the south of the plateau, are a UNESCO World Heritage site.

q.q: Which city on the plateau is called the 'City of Eternal Spring'?

Q874816.t: A shallow saucer of rice fields beside the Mekong
Q874816.s: North-east Thailand sits on the Khorat Plateau, a vast shallow saucer only about 100–200 m above the sea, tilted gently toward the Mekong. Its two main rivers, the Mun and the Chi, meander across it before joining the Mekong at the Lao border. From above look for a patchwork of rice paddies — bright green in the rainy season, gold and brown in the dry — dotted with villages and ponds.
Q874816.w: A flat patchwork of rice paddies and ponds, rimmed by low hills, with the Mekong curving along its northern and eastern edges.
f: Thick layers of rock salt lie beneath the plateau, and salt is still produced there.
Dinosaur fossils found at Phu Wiang made the plateau famous among palaeontologists.
The region, known as Isan, is home to about a third of Thailand's people.

q.q: Which great river bounds the Khorat Plateau to the north and east?

Q27696359.t: Myanmar's cool highland with a famous lake
Q27696359.s: East of the Irrawaddy plain, Myanmar climbs abruptly onto the Shan Plateau, a rolling upland around 1,000 m high, green with forest and fields. The Salween River slices through it in a deep gorge on its way to the sea. Look for Inle Lake, a long blue sliver in a valley, where villages stand on stilts and gardens float on the water.
Q27696359.w: A green, rolling upland rising sharply above the flat Irrawaddy plain, with long, narrow Inle Lake in a valley.
f: Inle Lake's fishermen are known for rowing with one leg wrapped around the oar.
The plateau's western edge rises as a steep escarpment above the central plain.
Taunggyi, capital of Shan State, lies at about 1,400 m near Inle Lake.

q.q: What are Inle Lake's fishermen famous for?

Q925906.t: Red-rock country where the Earth shows its layers
Q925906.s: The Colorado Plateau is one of the most spectacular things you can fly over: a high desert of red, orange and cream rock laid down in layers, then cut by rivers into canyons, mesas and buttes. The Grand Canyon, Monument Valley, Arches and Canyonlands all lie on it. On a clear day look for the winding blue arms of Lake Powell among bare red rock.
Q925906.w: Vast red-and-cream rock desert carved by winding canyons and flat-topped mesas, with the branching blue arms of Lake Powell.
f: The rocks exposed in the Grand Canyon span nearly two billion years of Earth's history.
It holds one of the greatest concentrations of national parks in the United States.
The Four Corners, where four US states meet, lies on the plateau.

q.q: Which great canyon on the plateau did the Colorado River carve?

Q401815.t: Lava floods and ice-age floods, written in the land
Q401815.s: Between the Cascades and the Rockies lies the Columbia Plateau, built from vast floods of basalt lava that poured out mostly 17 to 15 million years ago. At the end of the last ice age, colossal floods from a burst glacial lake raced across it and scoured the Channeled Scablands. From above look for the rolling, dune-like wheat hills of the Palouse and the broad blue curve of the Columbia River.
Q401815.w: Rolling golden wheat hills and bare, channel-scarred basalt, with the wide blue Columbia River curving through.
f: Some single lava flows travelled hundreds of kilometres, all the way to the Pacific.
The floods came from glacial Lake Missoula, which emptied again and again as its ice dam broke.
The rolling Palouse hills are made of wind-blown silt and farmed for wheat.

q.q: Floods from which ice-age lake carved the Channeled Scablands?

Q3623001.t: Gold-rush country along the Yukon River
Q3623001.s: Across central Yukon the land rolls away as the Yukon Plateau: forested uplands and broad valleys cut by the Yukon River and its tributaries. In 1896 gold was found in a creek near the Klondike River, and within two years tens of thousands of prospectors poured in. From above look for dark spruce, pale gravel bars and, in autumn, great swathes of yellow aspen and birch.
Q3623001.w: Rolling forested uplands cut by wide, braided river valleys, with the Yukon River winding north-west.
f: Parts of the plateau escaped the ice sheets of the last ice age, as part of Beringia.
Whitehorse, the Yukon's capital, stands on the plateau beside the Yukon River.
The Yukon River runs about 3,190 km to the Bering Sea.

q.q: Which gold rush brought prospectors here from 1896?

Q118574.t: The high plain of Titicaca and the great salt flat
Q118574.s: Between two chains of the Andes lies the Altiplano, a high plain averaging about 3,750 m — the most extensive high plateau on Earth after Tibet. From cruise it is an astonishing sight: brown steppe, snowy volcanoes along the rim, the deep blue of Lake Titicaca in the north and, in the south, the dazzling white of Salar de Uyuni, the largest salt flat in the world.
Q118574.w: A vast brown high plain ringed by snowy volcanoes, with a huge blue lake in the north and white salt flats to the south.
f: Salar de Uyuni covers about 10,000 km², and after rain it becomes a giant mirror.
Lake Titicaca, at about 3,810 m, is often called the highest navigable lake in the world.
Beneath the salt flats lie some of the world's largest known lithium reserves.

q.q: What is Salar de Uyuni?

ne-rg-1730071967.t: A lonely plateau in the heart of the eastern Sahara
ne-rg-1730071967.s: Far out in the eastern Sahara of north-western Sudan, the Jebel Abyad Plateau rises from the sand as a low, weathered tableland. Its name is Arabic for 'white mountain'. In a typical year hardly any rain falls here at all. From above look for dark rocky uplands streaked with wind-blown sand and, to the south, the faint winding line of Wadi Howar, a dry valley that was once a river.
ne-rg-1730071967.w: A dark, weathered tableland rising from pale sand, streaked by dunes, in the empty desert of north-western Sudan.
f: Wadi Howar, to the south, carried a Nile tributary when the Sahara was green, about 9,500–4,500 years ago.
Rock art across the eastern Sahara shows cattle and giraffes from that wetter time.

q.q: What does 'Jebel Abyad' mean in Arabic?

ne-rg-1730072941.t: A cerrado tableland named after a Brazilian classic
ne-rg-1730072941.s: West of the São Francisco River the land rises onto broad, flat cerrado tablelands laced with veredas — marshy valleys lined with buriti palms. This is the backcountry of João Guimarães Rosa's 1956 novel Grande Sertão: Veredas, and a national park carries its name. From above look for vast flat plateaus, many now covered in huge circles and rectangles of farmland, cut by green strips along streams.
ne-rg-1730072941.w: Vast flat tablelands of farmland and olive savanna, cut by dark green lines of palm-lined streams running east.
f: Guimarães Rosa's novel is often ranked among the greatest works of Brazilian literature.
Buriti palms, which line the veredas, can grow to about 30 m.
Its streams feed the São Francisco, the longest river lying entirely within Brazil.

q.q: Which writer's novel gave the Grande Sertão Veredas park its name?

Q1294308.t: Texas Hill Country, a limestone tableland of springs
Q1294308.s: West of Austin and San Antonio the land steps up onto the Edwards Plateau, a limestone tableland of ranches, oak and juniper scrub. Its southern and eastern edge is the Balcones Escarpment, where clear springs burst out at the foot of the slope. From above look for a grey-green plain crossed by tree-lined rivers, with the grids of Austin and San Antonio spread along the escarpment below.
Q1294308.w: A grey-green limestone tableland of scrub and ranches, dropping at its south-east edge toward Austin and San Antonio.
f: The Edwards Aquifer beneath its edge supplies most of San Antonio's drinking water.
Comal Springs, at New Braunfels, are among the largest springs in Texas.
Bracken Cave, near San Antonio, hosts one of the world's largest bat colonies.

q.q: Which city gets most of its water from the Edwards Aquifer?

ne-rg-1730072971.s: The Kazakh Uplands, known as Saryarka, fill the heart of Kazakhstan: a vast land of low, rounded hills, the worn stumps of ancient mountains, set in dry steppe. From above it looks like crumpled felt in shades of tan and olive, dotted with salt lakes. The coal city of Karaganda lies here, and to the south the long, thin Lake Balkhash marks the edge of the uplands.
ne-rg-1730072971.w: Crumpled tan and olive steppe with low rounded hills and salt lakes; the long, thin Lake Balkhash lies to the south.
f: The highest point, Aksoran, reaches about 1,565 m.
Lake Balkhash, to the south, is fresh in its western part and salty in the east.
Saryarka's steppe and lakes, including Korgalzhyn, are a UNESCO World Heritage site.

q.q: Which lake, fresh in the west and salty in the east, lies to the south?

ne-rg-1730072981.t: Rugged highlands north-east of Lake Baikal
ne-rg-1730072981.s: North-east of Lake Baikal, rugged ridges and deep basins make up the Stanovoy Highlands, a wild land of larch taiga and bare summits. The Baikal–Amur Mainline railway threads through them in tunnels and along valleys. In the Kodar Range, the highest part, small glaciers survive. Look out for a surprise in the Chara basin: a patch of golden sand dunes in the middle of the taiga.
ne-rg-1730072981.w: Rugged grey ridges and deep taiga-filled basins north-east of Baikal, with a small patch of golden sand dunes.
f: The Severomuysky Tunnel on the railway here, about 15 km long, is the longest in Russia.
The Kodar Range rises to about 3,070 m.
The Chara Sands cover a few dozen square kilometres, a real desert patch inside the taiga.

q.q: Which railway threads through the Stanovoy Highlands?

ne-rg-1730073599.t: Ancient rock and gold in southern Yakutia
ne-rg-1730073599.s: In southern Yakutia rise the Aldan Highlands, a rolling upland of taiga-covered hills built on some of the oldest rock in Asia. Gold was found here in 1923, and the rush that followed drew thousands of prospectors into the wilderness. From above look for dark larch forest, pale river valleys and, near Neryungri, the vast terraced pit of a coal mine cut into the hills.
ne-rg-1730073599.w: Rolling taiga-covered hills cut by pale river valleys, with a vast terraced open-pit mine near Neryungri.
f: The town of Aldan grew up during the gold rush of the 1920s.
The Amur–Yakutsk railway and the Lena highway both cross the highlands on their way north to Yakutsk.

q.q: What was found in the Aldan Highlands in 1923, sparking a rush?

Q1753873.t: A high desert tableland between two Sierras
Q1753873.s: Most of northern and central Mexico is a high tableland walled in by two mountain chains, the Sierra Madre Occidental to the west and the Sierra Madre Oriental to the east. Its northern part is the Chihuahuan Desert, all pale basins, dry lake beds and long ridges; farther south it rises and turns greener toward Mexico City. From above look for tan basins between parallel dark ranges.
Q1753873.w: Tan desert basins and white dry lake beds between parallel dark ridges, walled by higher mountains on both sides.
f: The Chihuahuan Desert is the largest hot desert in North America.
Mexico City lies on its southern part at about 2,240 m.
Copper Canyon, cut into its western rim, is deeper in places than the Grand Canyon.

q.q: Which mountains wall the Mexican Plateau to the west?

Q654947.t: Wooded hills and the long blue Finger Lakes
Q654947.s: Across southern New York and western Pennsylvania runs the Allegheny Plateau, an old tableland worn by rivers into a maze of steep wooded hills. On its northern edge, ice-age glaciers gouged the Finger Lakes, long, narrow and parallel as if scratched by a giant hand. From above they are unmistakable: a row of thin blue slivers running north–south.
Q654947.w: Wooded, deeply cut hills, with a row of long, narrow parallel lakes running north–south along the northern edge.
f: Seneca Lake, the largest of the Finger Lakes, is about 190 m deep at its deepest.
The first commercial oil well in the United States was drilled in 1859 at Titusville, on the plateau in Pennsylvania.

q.q: Which chain of long, narrow lakes lies on the plateau's northern edge?

Q1143656.t: A sandstone tableland of gorges and waterfalls
Q1143656.s: Rising above the Tennessee Valley, the Cumberland Plateau is a long sandstone tableland running from Kentucky through Tennessee into Alabama. Its flat, forested top ends in steep bluffs, and streams plunge off the edges into deep gorges. From above look for a dark green, flat-topped ridge with sharp escarpments, its rim notched by the V-shaped valleys of its waterfalls.
Q1143656.w: A long, flat-topped forested tableland with steep escarpments, its edges notched by deep, V-shaped gorges.
f: Fall Creek Falls, about 78 m high, is one of the highest waterfalls in the eastern United States.
At Cumberland Falls in Kentucky, a 'moonbow' can appear in the spray on clear full-moon nights.
Its hard sandstone cap resists erosion, which is why the plateau keeps its flat top.

q.q: What rare sight can appear at Cumberland Falls on full-moon nights?
